World.title: Appalachia's black lung rates highest in nearly 50 years as miners' protections stall
World.content:
Appalachia's black lung rates highest in nearly 50 years as miners' protections stall

toggle caption Roger May for NPR

Respiratory therapist Marcy Freeman doesn't need a research study to confirm for her a return to the dark days of coal mining. She finds evidence in a stack of more than 150 funeral programs, all for former patients at her pulmonary rehabilitation clinic in Norton, Virginia.

"Each one of these represents a life that's gone because of black lung," Freeman explained as she flipped through the programs, recognizing names and images.

"These are husbands. These are brothers. … These men were just hardworking men, and the only thing they did was go to work and provide for their families. And it cost them everything. … This is the aftermath of black lung."

Sponsor Message

toggle caption Justin Hicks/Louisville Public Media/LPM

This aftermath is more dire than even black lung clinicians and researchers expected, according to new data published Wednesday in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine.

The data appears in a peer-reviewed research letter from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), a federal research agency.

Public Health Watch, Kentucky Public Radio and NPR obtained a draft of the NIOSH research letter before publication.

NIOSH researchers found that working veteran underground coal miners in central Appalachia are suffering from the incurable and fatal lung disease at the highest rates in nearly 50 years.

Loading...

Miners working in Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia who've had at least 25 years underground have the worst rate of coal workers' pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease. One in three — 32.5% — tested positive in X-rays conducted by NIOSH during the last five years.

The last time the rate of disease was that high for miners with the same work history was 1978. In 2018, when NIOSH last reported rates of the disease, the rate was 20.6%.

The new research shows that even miners with as few as 15 years underground have higher rates of black lung — rates not seen in nearly 40 years.

"I'm disgusted," said Scott Laney, a NIOSH research epidemiologist who is the lead author of the research letter.

"This is not going to get better because of all the disease that's already in the pipeline. These guys are being treated like disposable widgets, not human beings. … We're watching them die right before our eyes."

More than 1,700 coal miners died from black lung from 2020 through 2023, according to an earlier NIOSH study.

Kentucky Public Radio and its reporting partners provided the federal Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) a summary of the NIOSH findings, but the agency declined to comment or respond to questions before seeing the published report.

"Coal miners are no better off"

The new findings "should stagger and shock anyone who has compassion for … hardworking people," said Celeste Monforton, a former federal mine-safety regulator and a workplace-safety academic and advocate.

"This is the consequence of their work and the consequence of us wanting cheap electricity," Monforton added. "We're back where we were [nearly 50 years ago]. … Coal miners are no better off than they were [then]."

Sponsor Message

The newly published findings do not include the number of miners tested or diagnosed in the five-year period used to determine the rate of disease. But in response to questions from Public Health Watch and Kentucky Public Radio, NIOSH said it screened 280 working veteran underground miners in central Appalachia in the past five years, with 91 testing positive for black lung. The agency used that sample to estimate a rate for all similar miners in the region, an approach used since 1974.

toggle caption Earl Dotter

"The overall process" that NIOSH researchers applied here "is valid in my opinion," said Akshay Sood, a clinical and research pulmonologist specializing in occupational lung diseases, including black lung, at the University of New Mexico School of Medicine. Sood reviewed a draft of the NIOSH research letter at the request of NPR, Kentucky Public Radio and Public Health Watch.

The NIOSH study "reinforces prior observations that disease prevalence continues to increase despite modern dust-control regulations," Sood concluded.

The NIOSH researchers also wrote that "multiple external indicators … demonstrate patterns consistent" with their findings, including thousands of new cases of disease diagnosed by black lung clinics in the last decade.

The new estimated rate for the veteran central Appalachian underground miners is more than a fourfold increase since the prevalence of the disease hit a low point: just 7%, in 1999. That was 22 years after Congress imposed strict limits on exposure to the coal mine dust that causes black lung.

toggle caption Earl Dotter

Since then, the dramatic plunge has reversed, especially in Appalachia, where thousands of miners are suffering from early, advanced and fatal stages of disease, according to data gathered from clinics testing and treating miners. Unlike NIOSH, which focuses on working miners, the clinics tend to see retired and laid-off miners who seek lung exams while trying to obtain state or federal black lung benefits.

Sponsor Message

The clinics have been inundated with miners in the wake of coal mine closures. More than 15,000 workers across the U.S. lost coal mine jobs in the last decade, according to employment data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

toggle caption Justin Hicks/Kentucky Public Radio

"It's awful," said Brandon Crum, a radiologist in Coal Run Village, Kentucky, who specializes in detecting signs of black lung in X-rays. In 2016, Crum first documented an alarming spike in severe black lung — as well as rapid progression of the disease — among younger and younger coal miners. NIOSH researchers and an NPR investigation confirmed his findings.

The new NIOSH research indicates to Crum that the trend continues.

"It's just another thing that proves what we've been saying for the last 10 years," he said. "And this may be even worse than what we thought it was going to be."

The National Mining Association (NMA), the leading industry trade group, was also provided a summary of the NIOSH findings. NMA noted that the rates of disease reported by NIOSH in miners tested in the last five years — along with the new cases diagnosed at clinics — do not stem from current silica dust exposures in coal mines because it can take years for disease to develop and for disease to be diagnosed.

"This means that the incidences discussed in these studies cover miners whose initial exposure dates back years and, in many cases, decades," Ashley Burke, a spokeswoman for NMA, wrote in an emailed statement. "These incidences do not reflect the conditions, practices, protections or regulations that are in place today."

Still, miner advocates are concerned that high rates of disease will continue because of a major change in coal mining that's causing dangerous dust exposure.

toggle caption Justin Hicks/Kentucky Public Radio

Cutting through rocks

In recent decades, the biggest coal seams in Appalachia were mined out. Mining companies turned to the thinner seams that remained, digging through mountains to reach and then mine them. That requires cutting lots of rock, and in Appalachia, that rock typically contains quartz, which is rich in silica. The result is clouds of both coal dust and highly toxic silica dust.

Sponsor Message

"Excessive inhalation of coal mine dust is the sole cause of [black lung] in coal miners," the new NIOSH research letter says. "Substantial evidence shows that exposure to the respirable crystalline silica component of coal mine dust plays an important role in contemporary disease patterns."

Laney, the NIOSH epidemiologist, said the link between silica dust and black lung disease is strong, based on exposure data and radiographic data, which shows abnormalities "suggestive of silica exposure." And he said researchers have inspected lungs removed in autopsies and after transplantation and "we can see the silica in these lungs."

toggle caption Roger May for NPR

toggle caption Justin Hicks/Kentucky Public Radio

Silica dust is 20 times more toxic than coal dust alone and contains fine particles that are easily inhaled. Silica particles cause lungs to fight back with fibrotic tissue that builds and builds, severely inhibiting the ability to breathe.

Coal miners who've worked underground in the last 25 years have witnessed the changes that led to more silica dust exposure.

"The thickness of the coal is not there," explained Tim Balthis, a former miner and mine foreman in Kentucky and Virginia. It's not like the days when the "grandpas" mined the big coal seams, he said. "So you're having to take more rock, which in turn creates silica dust."

Balthis spoke at New Beginnings Pulmonary Rehab, one of four black lung clinics owned and operated by Freeman, the respiratory therapist. The clinics help miners ease symptoms of the incurable disease.

At 57, Balthis has what is called complicated black lung, the advanced and fatal stage. He tried to describe for non-miners what it's like working around silica dust in an underground coal mine.

"It's like opening your front door and letting the sunshine [in]" with dust particles floating in the light. "And then multiply that by 10 billion times. … It's like a fog," Balthis recalled.

toggle caption Howard Berkes for NPR

"Thousands of opportunities for disease"

The National Mining Association cites government data that shows increasing compliance with silica dust exposure limits in the last 10 years, with mining companies nationwide meeting those limits more than 90% of the time. Last year, the compliance rate hit 97%.

Sponsor Message

But a high rate of compliance doesn't mean miners are fully protected. The small percentage of overexposures has translated to thousands of instances in which miners are put at risk.

Kentucky Public Radio and Public Health Watch analyzed MSHA silica dust sampling data and found that coal miners were exposed to excessive levels of silica dust more than 5,000 times since 2014. Silica particles are so toxic, so easily inhaled, and so easily embedded in lungs, that "thousands of exposures equate to thousands of opportunities for disease," said former regulator Monforton.

In fact, an NPR and FRONTLINE investigation in 2018 documented 21,000 instances of overexposure to silica dust in a review of 30 years of federal data. The news organizations also documented a growing number of retired and laid-off miners stricken with complicated black lung, a count that now exceeds 4,000 since 2010.

"A love affair with the black rock"

toggle caption Mine Safety and Health Administration

NIOSH first recommended tougher limits on silica dust exposure in coal mines in 1974. But for 50 years, both Democratic and Republican administrations failed to act. That finally changed in 2024, when the Biden administration succeeded in establishing a new silica dust regulation for mining. It made the exposure limit twice as restrictive. It also provided, for the first time, a direct regulatory response to overexposure, including imposition of even tougher exposure restrictions, and possible fines, for noncompliance.

But the mining industry sued, agreeing with the tougher exposure limit but not the enforcement mechanism.

Federal courts responded to the industry lawsuits, which also cite other issues, with an indefinite delay in enforcement of the tougher silica exposure limits. The Trump administration did not oppose the delay, announcing it too would put enforcement on hold.

And the Trump administration is trying to boost coal mining. In early June, Trump announced close to $700 million in federal spending to sustain coal-burning power plants and to support exports of coal.

"Coal's a great business," Trump said at the time. "In terms of power, there's nothing like it."

Monforton said the administration seems to have "a love affair with the black rock, and not a love affair or compassion or concern for coal miners."

Mining companies are required to control dust exposure with robust ventilation underground. Mining machines must also have water sprays that tamp down dust. But sometimes, they don't work well enough to keep the dust down.

Sponsor Message

The coal mining industry wants to be able to require the use of dust masks, so that miners could still work when other control measures fail.

"When other controls do not adequately reduce exposure levels, those extensive controls will be supplemented with respirators, which is no different than any other profession that requires the use of masks to ensure air quality safety." the NMA's Burke said.

But federal law treats underground coal mining differently from other industries. The Mine Safety and Health Act requires coal mining companies to prevent "unsafe and unhealthful conditions" and to make sure miners can work their entire careers in working conditions "sufficiently free of respirable dust" so they don't fall victim to black lung.

Dust masks and respirators have also been problematic. Many miners interviewed by NPR complained that masks impair communication in a dangerous and noisy environment, become clogged with dust, are too hot to work in, and fail to screen out finer particles. Lawsuits against dust-mask companies have resulted in multimillion-dollar verdicts and settlements.

toggle caption Roger May for NPR

Even more modern devices have issues, including helmets that push fresh air down across the face and behind a clear shield. MSHA noted in its 2024 silica dust regulation that the helmets "are not a permanent solution" because they make it difficult to communicate effectively, and may limit peripheral vision and situational awareness, which can make work hazardous.

Dr. Drew Harris, a University of Virginia pulmonologist, who is also medical director at the Stone Mountain black lung clinics in Virginia, is direct about delayed protections for coal miners.

"We need to act and we need the will to act," Harris asserted. "We need to enforce the protections that we know will work to make this disease go away."

"Folks that don't have a voice"

Harris' black lung clinics in southwestern Virginia, Stone Mountain Health Services, see more miners and diagnose more cases of disease than any clinic in the country. Miners from coal counties across Appalachia flock to Stone Mountain because it provides testing, treatment and legal help with black lung benefits claims.

Sponsor Message

Harris called the new findings from NIOSH "outrageous." But they're not surprising based on what he's been seeing in the clinics. In just the past five years alone, Stone Mountain has diagnosed 2,400 new cases of black lung.

"If you imagine one out of every three school teachers were getting an incurable lung disease because of something they were exposed to at work, the whole country would put their hands up screaming, and stop whatever this exposure was immediately," Harris said. "[But] this is largely impacting rural Appalachian folks that don't have a voice, that don't have a country to unite behind them."

The growing rate of disease has resulted in a steady stream of miners seeking state and federal benefits for living and medical expenses. More than 26,000 miners or their surviving dependents drew $175 million from a federal black lung trust fund in 2024, according to a Labor Department report to Congress.

Mining companies contributed more than $23 billion to the fund, according to NMA, but bankruptcies and underinsurance shift some of the burden to taxpayers. The fund owes more than $3 billion to the U.S. Treasury.

Public funds pay for most of a growing number of lung transplants, which cost as much as $2 million each, and are mostly for miners in central Appalachia, according to a NIOSH study.

toggle caption Roger May for NPR

The black lung burden for miners like Tim Balthis makes life itself challenging. Even the simplest tasks are difficult as fibrotic tissue builds up in his lungs. Breathing becomes more and more labored. He knows it will only get worse. He's likely to die from it, unless he qualifies for a lung transplant. But even that, for coal miners, comes with a median survival rate of less than seven years.

"It's like a cut in your manhood." Balthis said, noting that he carries and uses an "emergency inhaler" to get more than a few minutes of playing time with his grandchildren or even singing at church.

Sponsor Message

"I've had several doctors say that I should already be dead… And I tell them this…'God's not done with me yet.' I've been obedient to Him, and now He's giving me back to my grandbabies…He's not finished with me.'"

This story was produced as a collaboration between NPR; Public Health Watch, an independent nonprofit investigative newsroom focused on public, environmental and occupational health; Kentucky Public Radio; and the Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom.

World.title: MLS named LAFC co-owner Larry Berg as its next commissioner. Here's what to know
World.content:
MLS named LAFC co-owner Larry Berg as its next commissioner. Here's what to know

toggle caption Richard Drew/AP

Major League Soccer owners voted this week to name Los Angeles F.C. co-owner Larry Berg as their next commissioner — the man they hope will lead the league into the future and nearer to long-held ambitions of prominence among American sports fans and global soccer leagues.

Berg will officially become the first new MLS commissioner in 27 years on Jan. 1, 2027, after a transition period with outgoing head Don Garber.

In his decades on the job, Garber oversaw the league's glow-up from a cash-poor 10-team afterthought to the full-sized, mature league it is today, complete with 23 soccer-specific stadiums and youth academies for every team.

"I've experienced this sport as a player, a fan and owner, and now with tremendous humility as commissioner," Berg said at an introductory press conference Tuesday. "Every one of those experiences has reinforced the same belief: The future of Major League Soccer has never been brighter."

Sponsor Message

The transition comes at a pivotal moment for MLS, which is hoping for a boost to attendance and ratings in the wake of this summer's FIFA World Cup in North America. Next year, the league will shift its long-time season calendar to a summer-to-spring schedule to align with Europe's professional leagues. Ahead lie other challenges that have game-changing potential for the league, including looming labor negotiations and the expiration of the current media rights deal with Apple TV in 2029.

Around 125 candidates were considered for the job before owners voted among finalists this week to select Berg. His professional background is in private equity, and LAFC, the team he's been with since its founding in 2014, which is widely regarded as one of the most capably run franchises in MLS.

Read on for more:

Who is Larry Berg?

Berg is known best in the soccer world for his co-ownership of Los Angeles FC, which debuted in 2018 and has quickly become one of the league's most successful franchises. Under Berg's co-ownership, the team has won an MLS Cup and a U.S. Open Cup and has twice finished as the league's best regular-season team.

toggle caption David Berding/Getty Images

Berg has also served as co-chair of the league's Sporting and Competition Committee, the body that oversees rule changes, such as the forthcoming calendar switch. "That was way before he had the ambition to be commissioner, and he brought to that role an entirely modern and forward-thinking perspective as to where the product could be on the field," Garber said Tuesday.

Sponsor Message

What is his background?

Berg, who is 60, grew up playing soccer. On Tuesday, he recalled joining a youth league as an 8-year-old in his hometown of Cherry Hill, New Jersey, in 1974. (Back then, there were only two teams in the league, so they played each other every weekend, he joked.) He was an accomplished high school player who competed in a state championship against future Sporting KC head coach Peter Vermes. Berg was an early megafan of Major League Soccer who attended the Los Angeles Galaxy's inaugural home game in 1996.

Berg studied economics and business at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, and then at Harvard University. Ultimately, he pursued a career in private equity, becoming a senior partner at the firm Apollo Global Management, one of the world's largest private equity firms. Berg says he will divest his ownership stake in LAFC in order to take the job as commissioner.

Asked Tuesday about how his background in private equity would inform his approach to the job, Berg said he believed it would be an advantage. "It's about a sense of urgency. It's about rolling up the sleeves, being in the trenches, asking good questions, aligning people toward a common goal," he said.

toggle caption Elizabeth Ruiz Ruiz/Getty Images

What is Berg's vision for MLS?

In 2020, Berg boldly predicted that soccer and MLS would surpass baseball and hockey to become the No. 3 sport in the U.S. behind football and basketball. On Tuesday, he said he still believed in that vision.

(A recent Gallup poll found that professional soccer ranked in the middle of the pack when respondents were asked whether they were a fan of a wide variety of sports, including the major American professional and college sports, along with Olympic sports like figure skating. In terms of pro sports, soccer finished behind football, basketball and baseball but ahead of ice hockey, tennis and golf.)

Sponsor Message

"As we look ahead five to ten years from now, I hope people won't simply say that Major League Soccer got bigger. I hope they'll say it got better — better competition, better player development, stronger clubs, deeper connections with supporters, greater success internationally, and a league that inspired more young people across North America to fall in love with this game," Berg said Tuesday.

To accomplish all that, he said, the league must start by improving the quality of the on-field game.

"I would say that's my No. 1 job," he said. "We will have more transfer revenues, and we'll have more media money, and that'll all lead to better product on the field. And that will become a flywheel, because it leads to more transfers and more revenue money and more media money."

What are the big challenges ahead?

There's been a lot of chatter in the MLS world about the league's current roster rules and spending restrictions, with owners eager to simplify regulations and allow for more spending. Those changes will likely be subject to a negotiation with the MLS players' union, whose current contract is in place until Jan. 31, 2028.

toggle caption Ed Zurga/Getty Images

The other big item is the league's media rights deal. Right now, MLS earns about $250 million per year from Apple TV, the streaming provider that carries every MLS game (with some games simulcast on Fox and its suite of channels). League leadership believes that number could be significantly higher in the future.

"It's about finding media partners that want to co-create the future with us. It's about co-creating. It's about what's interesting to them, what's interesting to us," Berg said Tuesday. He raised the possibility of changing "certain things to [a media partner's] benefit," citing the controversial World Cup "hydration breaks" that allowed broadcasters to air valuable commercials during games.

Sponsor Message

What does he think about promotion and relegation?

This one's for the soccerheads.

Some vocal fans have called for implementing a Europe-style promotion-relegation system in U.S. soccer. Supporters of the idea believe it would incentivize lower-performing teams to remain competitive to avoid relegation to a lower division. Investors and team owners generally oppose the idea, because relegation can be a financial disaster for teams, and they want to protect their multimillion-dollar investments.

On Tuesday, Berg was directly asked about the idea.

"I don't think it's a great way to build the league. I don't think it's a way to get stadiums built and to get training facilities built and to have owners invest in rosters and all the other things you need to do," he said. "I just don't see it happening any time soon."

World.title: Authorities arrested a man with ammo and apparently monitoring security at Trump golf course near LA
World.content:
Authorities arrested a man with ammo and apparently monitoring security at Trump golf course near LA

toggle caption John Antczak/AP

RANCHO PALOS VERDES, California — A man carrying ammunition and with a gun in his car was arrested Sunday at President Donald Trump's Los Angeles-area golf course after appearing to monitor security preparations two days ahead of Trump's fundraiser there, authorities said Tuesday.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket. Authorities recovered a loaded pistol in his car. Law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey on Monday and found a plethora of firearms, magazines and ammunition, body armor and notebooks with "concerning statements."

Sponsor Message

The sheriff's department announced the arrest as Trump was preparing to arrive for a fundraising dinner for the Republican National Committee at the Trump National Golf Course in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes just south of Los Angeles.

Taele was charged with several felonies including second-degree robbery, receiving a large-capacity magazine and possession of a short-barreled rifle or shotgun. He was also charged with carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, a misdemeanor.

He pleaded not guilty to all the charges Monday and was ordered to stay away from the golf course and not possess weapons. His bail was set at $250,000.

It wasn't clear if he had an attorney, and family members could not immediately be reached for comment.

The sheriff's department said when they made contact with Taele on Sunday, they had determined he was being investigated by the El Segundo Police Department for robbery.

The sheriff's department said there is "no credible threat to our communities."

A jury in 2025 found a man guilty of trying to assassinate Trump at the president's Florida country club.

World.title: Russia unleashes deadly wave of missiles, drones on Kyiv
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding area left 17 people dead and dozens more injured. The latest Russian strikes come as Ukraine struggles with a limited number of key interceptors.

Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region killed 17 people and wounded 44 others overnight into Wednesday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The attack was the latest in a series of large-scale Russian ballistic missile strikes that have become near-routine this summer. The intensified barrages are exploiting Ukraine's critical shortage of interceptor missiles for the U.S.-made Patriot systems, the sole air defence system in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles.

Zelenskyy has pleaded with other countries to send more of the ammunition made scarcer by the Iran war.

"Ballistic interceptors are what could have saved the lives of those killed today," Zelenskyy said on social media. "It is very important for our partners to understand that delays in supplying them, or a reluctance to hand over anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction."

Large warehouse fires burned in the city of Brovary and the villages of Velyka Dymerka, Kvitneve and Peremoha. (Anatolii Stepanov/Reuters)

Russia fired 24 ballistic missiles, four other missiles identified as either hypersonic Zircons or supersonic Oniks, and 115 drones, many of them jet-powered, in the attack.

Zelenskyy said the strikes mainly targeted warehouses belonging to civilian businesses, as well as infrastructure and a railway station, hitting sites that he described as "with no connection to the war"— including a brewing company, building materials warehouses and civilian logistics facilities.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's president on defence technology development, said the war of attrition has entered a new phase.

"The enemy is attacking everything indiscriminately — retail warehouses, food storage facilities, logistics hubs, enterprises, building materials warehouses," he said on Facebook.

Canadian-designed armour for women put to the test in Ukraine | Duration 2:16 Female soldiers on Ukraine’s front lines are testing new armour designed by a Canadian company to better fit and protect women’s bodies.

Russia says it hit war-supporting companies

The Russian Defence Ministry said it struck transport, logistics and distribution centres involved in military activity. It listed four targets in Kyiv, claiming they ran war-related operations.

It was not immediately possible to reconcile the different accounts.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strikes mainly targeted warehouses belonging to civilian businesses, as well as infrastructure and a railway station. (Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images)

Ukraine's largest private postal operator, Nova Poshta, said a Russian cluster munition destroyed one of its sorting centres in Kyiv.

The Russian Defence Ministry said the centre was "storing and distributing dual-use goods, including those used in the production of long- and medium-range uncrewed aerial vehicles, as well as robotic systems and electronic warfare systems." It claimed that two other logistics centres in the Kyiv region stored drones or components for drones.

Separately, the ministry said its forces hit three bulk carriers on the Black Sea south of Odesa that it claimed were transporting weapons and military equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces. Ukrainian officials didn't comment on that claim.

One of the companies that came under heavy fire was the Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest retail and construction chains. It said in a statement on Facebook that "in minutes, Russian missiles destroyed what the company had built over decades."

Firefighters put out a fire Wednesday after Russian missiles hit a food warehouse near Kyiv. (Efrem Lukatsky/The Associated Press)

One employee was killed and three others were wounded. Russia hit two of the company's key logistics hubs.

According to the Russian Defence Ministry, the Epicentr site handled order processing, sorting, storing and delivery of dual-use goods and components for drone production.

Ukraine fires hundreds of drones

In its latest attack on logistics facilities of Wildberries, Russia's biggest online retailer, Ukrainian drones hit a warehouse in the Tula region south of Moscow, the company and the region's governor said Wednesday.

It was the 14th Wildberries warehouse to catch fire in less than three weeks, according to a Ukrainian tally. Ukraine says the company provides goods that can be used by the military. Kyiv is also keen to unsettle the Russian public with high-profile attacks.

Why attack 'Russia's Amazon'? | About That | Duration 1:45 Andrew Chang explains why Ukraine is carrying out drone attacks on warehouses owned by Wildberries — Russia's most profitable online retailer. (Photo credits: Wildberries, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

The Russian Defence Ministry said its forces downed 475 Ukrainian drones overnight over 16 Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

U.S.-led peace efforts to end the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022 have apparently stalled. Trump, at a NATO summit in Turkey last month, teased a plan for Ukraine to produce missile systems with U.S. defence contractors, but no details have followed and such a plan wouldn't be of immediate help.

World.title: Veteran Canadian broadcaster Lloyd Robertson dead at 92
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Lloyd Robertson, who delivered the news to Canadians in an authoritative and unflappable manner for more than 40 years as anchor for the flagship news programs of CTV and CBC, has died. He was 92.

His death was first reported by CTV and was confirmed by a family member to CBC News.

Robertson stepped away as CTV National News anchor in 2011 after 35 years, having joined the network in a move from CBC that reshaped Canadian broadcast news. He had been anchor of CBC's The National for six years.

"Someone came along with this … on my terms, in my life at precisely the right moment, and it was irresistible. I couldn't turn it down," he told CBC's Take 30 in 1976, days after accepting the offer.

At CTV, Robertson helped lead coverage of 11 federal elections, three Canadian-hosted Olympic Games and two Quebec referendums, as well as tragedies like the 1985 Air India bombing, 1989 Montreal massacre and the Sept. 11 attacks. He also helped share inspiring stories such as Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope.

WATCH | Robertson announces retirement: Lloyd Robertson retires | Duration 3:50 CTV anchor stepping down after decades-long career, including 22 years at CBC

Robertson frequently spoke of enjoying being at the centre of attention for events shaping Canada and the world, but his on-air style was once accurately described as "self-effacing and lacking in the watch-me swagger of most news anchors," by Globe and Mail television critic John Doyle.

Robertson was "the guy with the smallest ego I've ever seen in the television business, when he has a right to the largest one," Henry Kowalski, former CTV news chief, told the same newspaper in 2001.

"He was not just a fine journalist but a fine person," said Peter Mansbridge, former chief correspondent for CBC News, describing Robertson as a "friend and colleague of mine for more than 50 years.

"His audience believed him, and they trusted him. He set the bar for those who anchored newscasts across the country, and he will always be remembered for that.”

In addition to a number of industry awards during his career, he was inducted as an officer into the Order of Canada in 1997 and into the Canadian News Hall of Fame for the Canadian Journalism Foundation in 2016.

"If you find something that you love to do, and you're able to do it, that's about as good as it gets in life," Robertson said in a 2012 CTV documentary And That's the Life I Led.

WATCH | Robertson reports on new skateboarding fad in 1965: The scoop on 'skurfing' | Duration 2:19 The teenage president of the Ontario branch of the National Sidewalk Surfers of Canada explains her organization's reason for being.

Robertson was born in Stratford, Ont., on Jan. 19, 1934, to parents George and Lilly, the youngest of their two children by nine years. He also had eight older half-siblings from the first marriage of his father, whose ancestors emigrated from Scotland in the mid-19th century.

He hung on the advice and political musings of his father, a Canadian National Railway machinist, and the pair enjoyed radio comedies together.

But it was often a "dreary home life," he wrote in his 2012 memoir The Kind of Life It's Been, owing to his British mother's struggles with mental illness. Prone to bouts of paranoia and obsessive-compulsive behaviour, she would be lobotomized when he was 14, quelling her mind to a degree but dulling her emotional connection with her son.

"I couldn't have kids to the house, I couldn't tell them about her," he told CBC's George Stroumboulopoulos Tonight in 2012.

WATCH | Mansbridge surprises Robertson on Strombo:

High school classmates, in the 2012 CTV documentary that accompanied his memoir, remembered a friend who gave little sign of turmoil. Robertson was popular, participating in debate and a barbershop quartet at Stratford Central Secondary School.

22-year run at CBC

Already gifted with a smooth voice, he'd been intrigued by radio after standing near reporters covering a post-war parade in his hometown in 1946.

"I just remember being fascinated by the voices of the two commentators as they painted vivid pictures of the marchers and the joyous crowds," he wrote in his memoir.

At just 17, he persuaded Stratford radio station CJCS to give him an opportunity, overcoming an early on-air bungled pronunciation of the city name as "Strat-herd."

He didn't consider going beyond high school, learning the craft of radio at private stations in Stratford and Guelph, before beginning a 22-year run with the public broadcaster in 1954 in Windsor.

WATCH | Robertson anchors CBC in 1970: Lloyd Robertson, rookie news anchor | Duration 1:43 Lloyd Robertson was an anchor at the CBC before he became the face of CTV News.

For Robertson, 1956 was a momentous year — his elderly father died just months after he landed at CBC Winnipeg for his first foray into television.

That year he also married Nancy Barrett, a high school sweetheart with whom he had remained in touch. The couple would welcome four daughters born in Winnipeg, Ottawa and Toronto, reflecting Robertson's peripatetic, upward climb.

In his memoir, he remembered his four-plus years in Winnipeg as "among my happiest and most productive," and he even donned Western garb to host the country-flavoured Saddle Songs. He then honed political chops with a two-year stint with CBC Ottawa — though it wasn't all Parliament Hill business, as he hosted a show about the CFL's Ottawa Rough Riders.

Robertson stands with his star at Canada's Walk of Fame in Toronto in June 2007. (Mark Blinch/Reuters)

In 1962 came an offer from the corporation the couple couldn't refuse, and another move. Robertson would remember being at the "bottom of the pile" of 30 announcers, all male, at CBC Toronto.

Robertson would separate himself over time, displaying adaptability by hosting a kid's show, the athletics program Kaleidosport, and a host of news and magazine programs. Many Canadian radio listeners first heard of John F. Kennedy's assassination in 1963 from Robertson, and he would score high-profile network assignments for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and Expo '67 in Montreal.

Robertson was cool and collected on air, but admitted years later that co-anchoring the 1969 moon shot by U.S. astronauts gave him pause.

Robertson is seen in Toronto in December 2001. (Aaron Harris/The Canadian Press)

"I had to pinch myself to be sure I was really living through this momentous time," he wrote.

Robertson would be rewarded with the network's plum assignment of anchoring The National in late 1970. It was a baptism by fire, as within days the Front de libération du Québec would plunge the province and country into crisis, kidnapping British diplomat James Cross and ultimately killing provincial minister Pierre Laporte.

CBC's news and current affairs roster was deep in the first years of that decade — future Canadian news anchors Peter Kent, Peter Trueman, Peter Mansbridge and Jan Tennant, along with budding stars like Adrienne Clarkson, Barbara Frum and Alex Trebek.

But there were also increasingly outdated union strictures involving studio and field work. Robertson once shared his workplace frustrations with Walter Cronkite on a trip to U.S. He recounted that the CBS news titan was incredulous that CBC anchors couldn't write their own copy, and were limited in reporting outside of the studio.

Move to CTV

In a time where NBC and ABC were employing multi-anchor formats in the U.S., Robertson was promised more freedom upon joining CTV National News in 1976, even as Harvey Kirck remained on the desk.

"Life with Harvey was sometimes tumultuous, occasionally precarious, but never dull," he wrote in his memoir of a co-anchor he described as loyal, but who caused the news division headaches with impaired driving citations.

Robertson adjusted to private-sector reality — more commercials, and local affiliates with clout — but he was welcomed by colleagues.

WATCH | Robertson on why he moved to CTV: Career change for Lloyd Robertson | Duration 1:39 The CBC's Larry Stout learns why money wasn't the only thing that motivated Lloyd Robertson to leave CBC for CTV. Aired on CBC's The National on June 21, 1976.

"What Lloyd did is [he] gave us instant credibility, and our numbers began to climb, and we've never retreated, really," said Craig Oliver, a top CTV political reporter and off-air friend, in 2012.

Kirck's departure in 1984 established Robertson's pre-eminence. Around the same time, coincidentally, he was approached by the Conservative Party to run as an MP. He wrote years the prospect held "some appeal," but he rebuffed that entreaty, and one by the Liberal Party in the early 2000s to serve as a senator.

By the 1990s, Roberton was ending the newscast with what would become a trademark: "And that's the kind of day it's been." He was firmly established as an éminence grise in the industry, winning three Geminis that decade for best host, anchor or interviewer.

Robertson initiated a plan to step back from anchoring in 1996 and give way to CTV reporter Keith Morrison, but, he wrote years later, it imploded due to a combination of corporate resistance and misunderstandings. He expressed regret that the personal relationship with Morrison was ruptured beyond repair.

Robertson would still be in the anchor chair in the next decade and beyond, pulling a 14-hour shift on Sept. 11, 2001, the day of the terrorist attacks on U.S. soil by Islamist militants.

"The magnitude of this crisis is truly breathtaking," he told viewers. He admitted to The Canadian Press that days later his voice "may have been trembling a little bit," describing the scene as tens of thousands who had gathered on Parliament Hill for several minutes of silence in honour of what would be nearly 3,000 innocent victims, including 24 Canadians.

PHOTOS | Robertson through the years:

Robertson tributes flowed in 2010, and the year after, as he gave a year's notice of his intention to leave the anchor post.

"I've never seen Lloyd angry," Kent, then a federal politician, marvelled at the time. "Lloyd is a gentleman and a paragon of integrity."

Robertson remained with the network for several more years, contributing to investigative program W5, and he continued charitable work that included raising awareness of mental illness.

He was able to spend more time with his children and grandchildren, who were used to that sometimes-booming baritone.

"There's a line that we use: 'Dad, I'm in the room,'" daughter Susan Robertson told CTV in 2012. "But that's his trademark, that's his voice."

While straight-laced on air, Robertson wasn't overly fussy with his image, appearing in comedic skits with the Royal Canadian Air Farce, and with Drake in a taped segment for the Juno Awards. As to SCTV's newscaster "Floyd Robertson," he told CBC he thought the portrayal by Joe Flaherty was "marvelous."

World.title: In Gaza City, a funeral for 112 family members takes place 3 years after their deaths
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Between mounds of rubble and shells of buildings in Gaza City, more than 100 orange stretchers were draped in Palestinian flags Tuesday morning — it was the site of an Israeli airstrike that took place at the start of the war.

Some flags were smaller, indicating the remains belonged to children. Photos rested atop some of the makeshift shrouds, while others were strewn with flower petals. It took almost three years to retrieve these remains, now reduced to bones, teeth and bits of clothing.

They belong to 112 members of the Abu Sharia and Hasayna families, members of the same clan, who were killed in the Nov. 23, 2023, Israeli airstrike on the neighbourhood where they lived.

WATCH | Mourners bury 112 family members in Gaza funeral 3 years after deaths: 'A wound that has opened again': Gaza burials take place 3 years on | Duration 1:57 Mourners gathered on Tuesday in a Gaza City neighbourhood where it's taken nearly three years to retrieve the remains of 112 people killed by an Israeli airstrike. Surviving members of the Abu Sharia and Hasayna families said they've long been looking alongside Gaza's Civil Defence for their loved ones, but a lack of heavy machinery in the war-torn territory has slowed their efforts.

Hundreds of people, including surviving family members, gathered on Tuesday morning to pray for the dead as they were laid to rest at the nearby Baptist cemetery.

Members of the families say they've been looking for their loved ones for years alongside Gaza's Civil Defence, first responders who attend strike sites to look for survivors and later retrieve remains. But the process has been slow due to a lack of heavy machinery in the strip.

Mahmoud Hasayneh, who was there to bury his brothers, says it opened old wounds for the family.

"Now we will start a new broken heart with this mission and all our family is crying," he said.

Heavy machinery needed

Last month, Youssef Abu Sharia, 23, was at the strike site waiting with baited breath as an excavator worked slowly, digging through piles of dirt and metal to try to retrieve any human remains that might be buried beneath the rubble.

Some of the heavy machinery in the strip has been damaged in Israeli strikes , and the United Nations said last month that Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy equipment into the enclave has hampered efforts to locate remains.

Abu Sharia lost his mother, father, brother and cousins in the November strike. He's been looking for their remains for years, but the process has been slow due to this lack of equipment.

He and his family decided to split up sometime in October 2023 when the war began to avoid the possibility of the entire family dying in one strike.

Abu Sharia and some of his cousins moved to a different part of the strip, while his parents and brother remained together with other relatives in Gaza City. Soon after, they were killed in the strike.

Mourners gather for a funeral for 112 people in Gaza City on Tuesday. It took almost three years to retrieve the remains, now reduced to bones, teeth and bits of clothing. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

At Tuesday's funeral, he said he felt relief that they could finally bury their loved ones following "three years of waiting day after day and moment after moment." He said there was also frustration and sadness over "a wound that has opened again."

His relative, Tayseer Abu Sharia, who was also at the funeral, says the last few years have been difficult as they waited for the Civil Defence to help find their loved ones.

Eventually, he says, they took matters into their own hands — literally digging through dirt and rubble "using our nails and hands."

The Civil Defence and human rights groups have called on Israel to allow heavy equipment into Gaza to help excavate bodies from the rubble.

Thousands still missing in Gaza

At least 7,400 people remain under the rubble in Gaza, Zaher al-Waheidi, head of the health ministry’s records department told The Associated Press.

The true number is likely thousands higher , he said, because in some cases entire families were killed in a single attack, leaving no one to report the missing.

Mahmoud Basal, the Civil Defence spokesperson, was at Tuesday's funeral where he urged the international community to act to get machinery into the strip.

"The difficulties we face are very big, there are no resources, no tools, no equipment," he said.

Basal said Tuesday's funeral was the first time in the history of the Palestinian cause that people have had to attend a funeral for 112 people.

Dozens of children were among the remains of 112 members of two families buried in Gaza City Tuesday. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

A long-awaited burial

Tuesday's ceremony began with a prayer over the flag-covered remains at the strike site.

Then, members of the crowd picked up the shrouds and carried them in a procession to the cemetery as onlookers tossed flower petals.

Chants and prayers filled the air as the Abu Sharia and Hasayneh families finally brought their loved ones to their final resting place.

As Youssef Abu Sharia and his surviving family members watched the burial, they could not help but think of those who are still missing.

"We cannot find any trace of them, we don’t see their bodies, we don’t see bones," he said. "Where did they go?"

World.title: Filipino tennis star Alex Eala riding a wave of popularity into Toronto tournament
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When rising Filipino tennis star Alex Eala plays on Canadian soil at the National Bank Open in Toronto, she'll be on centre court in front of a sold out crowd of 10,000.

The moment Eala's appearance was announced — a second round Wednesday night match — seats sold out within 30 minutes, according to Karl Hale, tournament director for the NBO, Canada's biggest tennis tournament and one of the most prestigious on the WTA tour.

"We've never seen a player ranked outside the top five have this type of effect," Hale said. "I think her fans were specifically waiting to see when she played."

And it's not just happening in Toronto.

The WTA tour is a gruelling season of more than 50 tournaments across dozens of countries, spanning multiple continents. And with every appearance, Eala's fans seem to find her.

"All the tournament directors are talking about it, everybody in the industry is talking about it," said Hale.

Eala's popularity has been driven by a massive Filipino diaspora, but also the vitality of her dramatic wins and charismatic interviews. She's a fresh face on the tour that has looked for star power following the retirement of big names like Serena Williams.

Eala kisses the championship trophy after winning the women's singles championship match at the Mubadala D.C. Open 2026, making her the first tennis player from the Philippines to bag a WTA title. (Scott Taetsch/Getty Images)

But with that growing popularity has come some backlash, with some online critics calling her overhyped.

However, Eala will play in Toronto fresh off a historic win at the Mubadala D.C. Open in Washington, D.C., making her the first tennis player from the Philippines to bag a WTA title.

"She's now 20 in the world. So she is really backing it up and she's growing her fan base," said Hale.

Big crowds at all tournaments

The early seeds of that fandom came when Eala reached the semifinals of another prestigious WTA tournament in 2025, the Miami Open. She beat out big names, including two top five players.

From there, the crowds only got bigger, extending even to the Grand Slams — the four biggest tournaments of the tennis season.

At last year's U.S. Open in New York, an energized crowd gave her first-round match the feel of a more consequential clash. Eala came from behind to win, marking the first time a player from the Philippines won a Grand Slam match.

From there, the so-called Eala effect seemed to catch.

Fans lined up for hours to catch her in the first round of this year's Australian Open in Melbourne. At the time, Eala was ranked 49th and lost that first match.

Her fans carried flags, signs and cheered so loud, it was noted by the opponent who beat her, American Alycia Parks.

After the match, Parks said, "It was difficult," mentioning that Eala definitely had a good crowd.

Then at Wimbledon in London, the crowd roared when she upset the defending champ Iga Swiatek in the third round.

"It is incredible to have my countrymen cheering me on, knowing that we are all in this together," Eala said in the post-match interview .

American tennis star turned-podcaster Andy Roddick has called it "Eala-mania."

On his podcast, he said: "Eala-mania is fun! When you have watch parties in arenas around your country for a fourth-round match, I'm in."

A new kind of tennis star

Eala's popularity signals a shift in tennis that many have long called for — more diversity.

The top-ranked players in the sport are concentrated in North America and Europe, with the dominant clusters in the U.S., Russia, Spain and France.

Asia has had few players break through the top ranks, while the Philippines, a country of 100 million people, has never produced a tennis star before.

Eala has noted this, embracing her Filipino fans and speaking in her native tongue often during her tournament interviews.

Alex Eala serves in a match at the U.S. Open in New York City in August 2025. (Kris Reyes/CBC)

As a Filipino Canadian tennis fan, I can speak to that pride. My whole family has been following Eala since she won the junior's girls title at the U.S. Open in 2022, excited at the prospect of cheering for another Filipino in a sport we already loved.

And there is a kind of thrill, hearing words like laban, the Tagalog word for fight, shouted from the stands at international tournaments.

It is a joy to watch an entire country, the Filipino diaspora and the rest of the tennis world get excited to walk alongside Eala in pursuit of bigger titles, even a Grand Slam trophy.

Eala's rise has put her on the cover of every major publication in her country, from Vogue to Tatler, while garnering congratulations from Filipinos everywhere in the world, including the Philippine president.

"Everywhere around the world, we have been watching you. We've been willing you on, and we have been so proud of you," President Bongbong Marcos said at a reception hosted for the athlete at the nation's presidential palace.

She's credited the love and support of her country for motivating her to continue battling on the court.

In an interview in 2022 with the WTA , she explained why she considers it a privilege to be a banner holder for the Philippines.

"It's important to me because I don't see a lot of Filipinos on the worldwide tennis stage."

World.title: Father pushes daughter's wheelchair 200 km to Toronto to advocate for access to health care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A London, Ont., father has begun a six-week walk to Queen's Park in Toronto, pushing his daughter's empty wheelchair 200 kilometres to advocate for easier access to out-of-country health care.

Joe Gesualdi set out Tuesday morning from his home in south London, pushing the wheelchair to Victoria Park, the first four kilometres of a journey he hopes will draw the attention of politicians and the public to his daughter Sydney's struggle to access treatment.

Sydney Gesualdi was 24 when she was rear-ended at a red light in July 2023. She was initially diagnosed with whiplash and soft-tissue injuries, but in the weeks that followed, she lost the ability to walk, began struggling to breathe and experienced numbness in her face and limbs.

Now 27, she is seeking surgery in New York that she says could improve her condition, but the family says it cannot afford the cost.

WATCH | Day 1 of the Miles4AMiracle walk: Dad walks from London to Queens Park to share daughter's health story | Duration 1:22 Joe Gesualdi started his Miles4AMiracle walk Tuesday morning, pushing his daughter Sydney's empty wheelchair from his home in south London to Victoria Park downtown. It's the first few kilometres of what will be a 200-kilometre walk to Queens Park in Toronto, where the father will share his daughter's story and advocate for easier access to out-of-country health care. He tells CBC News what's at stake and why he's up for the challenge.

"This wheelchair of Sydney's represents everything that has been taken away from her young life," Joe Gesualdi explained.

"It's out of desperation that I made the decision to walk her wheelchair 200 kilometres as a symbol of my commitment to Sydney, my love for her and to regain the possibility she will have a normal life again.

"I can't give up on Sydney, and I'm hoping that this change comes."

Sydney has been diagnosed with cranio-cervical instability, a condition involving excessive movement between the skull and the top two vertebrae in the neck. She says her symptoms have worsened over the past year and now include memory loss, choking and slurred speech.

"I'm essentially housebound. I spend 80 per cent of the day horizontal or sitting in bed," she said. "I only really am able to leave my house for necessary medical appointments, so my life has become very small."

Sydney Gesualdi, now 27, was rear-ended at a red light in July 2023. Since then, she's lost the ability to walk, struggles to breathe and swallow, and experiences extreme fatigue, among other symptoms. (Submitted by Sydney Gesualdi)

"I am just continuing to deteriorate without care and my symptoms are becoming more and more concerning as each week and month passes," she said.

"I'm just scared and I don't want to die."

Last year, Sydney told CBC News about her struggle to receive a spinal assessment. She was referred to eight doctors at spinal clinics across the province but had been denied consultations, with centres at the time citing wait times and heavy caseloads as reasons for not taking a patient.

The family eventually consulted a neurosurgeon in New York, who recommended surgery costing more than $49,000 CAD.

The Ontario Ministry of Health denied Sydney's application for full funding through its Out-of-Country Health Services program, leaving the family to raise the money themselves.

"Sydney's condition has deteriorated, and if we wait too long, she may not benefit from the surgery," Joe Gesualdi said. "I can't wait any longer for the process to play out."

Advocacy along the way

As he makes his way to Toronto, Gesualdi is handing out flyers explaining Sydney's story, encouraging donations toward the surgery and raising awareness about the challenges some Ontarians face when seeking medical treatment outside Canada.

He said he hopes the walk will also capture the attention of Premier Doug Ford, the Ministry of Health and other decision-makers.

"The more people that understand what's going on and they connect that to their own family stories is going to help advance the ball and bring meaningful change," he said.

Father Joe Gesualdi (left) is handing out flyers on his walk to Queens Park, sharing the details about his daughter Sydney Gesualdi's story and advocating for more accessible out-of-country healthcare treatment. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)

Sydney said she's appreciative of her dad going on the walk, as well as her mom's help planning the route.

"I feel very lucky, but at the same time, it's almost a mixed bag of emotions because I feel sad that it's come to this point where my dad has to do this for me to access medical care that with hopefully have a very positive outcome," she said.

Joe Gesualdi said he expects the walk to be challenging, but it doesn't live up to what his daughter faces daily.

"I am going to walk every single mile, every kilometre. There's not going to be any shortcuts," he said.

"Yes, it's going to be a long walk but the reality is that with Sydney's need for care, that never takes a break."

World.title: Multi-use path opens at Gordie Howe International Bridge as dozens line up to be first to cross
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Pedestrians and cyclists have begun crossing the Gordie Howe International Bridge.

The bridge's multi-use path opened at 8 a.m. on Wednesday.

The Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority (WDBA) is asking people to be patient as they wait for their turn.

“With the anticipated high number of path users, expect line-ups entering the path and line-ups at border processing,” it wrote on its website.

“WDBA is limiting the number of people that can be on the path at any one time over the initial opening days to support smooth operations.”

The bridge authority has set up porta-potties outside the entrance to the path.

Porta-potties, balloons, merchandise on site

They also have a covered booth with balloons on hand and bridge merchandise for sale.

By 7:50 a.m., around 70 people were lined up at the gate, separated from the roadway by yellow tape stretched between orange stanchions.

The bridge authority estimates it will take people approximately 45 minutes to make the three-kilometre trek on foot from one border inspection booth to the other.

It estimates the same trip will take around 20 minutes by bike.

A line-up forms at the entrance to the multi-use path at the Gordie Howe International Bridge Aug. 5, 2026. (Pratyush Dayal/CBC)

There is a posted speed limit on the trail of 20 kilometres per hour.

Both the bridge authority and the Canada Border Services Agency are reminding people to bring their travel documents onto the bridge even if they aren’t planning to cross into the United States.

Path-users who return to the Canadian side of the bridge will have to report to the Canada Border Services Agency before exiting, the agency said, and people without proper documentation could be held up while officials try to verify their identity and status.

The bridge authority is also reminding people that there is no on-site parking at either port of entry and is advising people to park at the Malden Park trailhead in Windsor or the Clark Park trailhead in Detroit.

World.title: Man charged after allegedly bringing gun, ammo to Trump's golf course ahead of presidential visit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A man carrying ammunition and with a gun in his car was arrested Sunday at U.S. President Donald Trump's Los Angeles-area golf course after appearing to monitor security preparations two days ahead of Trump's fundraiser there, authorities said Tuesday.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket. Authorities recovered a loaded 9mm pistol in his car. Law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey on Monday and said they found firearms, ammunition, body armour and notebooks with "concerning statements."

The sheriff's department announced the arrest as Trump was preparing to arrive for the Republican National Committee dinner at the Trump National Golf Course in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes just south of Los Angeles.

Taele's "troubling behaviour … raised serious red flags for law enforcement," Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles office, said in a statement. "There is no room for error, particularly in light of previous attempts on President Trump's life."

Taele was charged with several felonies including second-degree robbery, receiving a large-capacity magazine and possession of a short-barrelled rifle or shotgun. He was also charged with carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, a misdemeanour.

He pleaded not guilty to all the charges Monday and was ordered to stay away from the golf course and not possess weapons. His bail was set at $250,000 US.

It wasn't clear if he had an attorney, and family members could not immediately be reached for comment.

Members of the U.S. Secret Service watch before the Marine One helicopter, with Trump on board, lands near the golf club on Tuesday. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

Ahead of Tuesday's event, federal agents conducted a security assessment on Friday at the golf course. A person later identified as Taele was seen walking throughout the course, wore an earpiece and took photographs and videos of federal agents' activities, authorities said.

Taele drove away but then returned to the course Sunday. He approached federal agents and said he was employed by the State Department and was there for a security detail. Taele said he had a loaded weapon in his vehicle and was arrested after it was searched, according to federal officials.

Earlier this year, an armed man from North Carolina was shot dead by Secret Service agents after driving into the secure perimeter of Mar-a-Lago, Trump's resort in Palm Beach, Fla.

Meanwhile, a 31-year-old California man faces charges including attempting to assassinate the president after being arrested armed and running near a security checkpoint before Trump's appearance in April at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner at the Washington, D.C., Hilton hotel.

In February, a 60-year-old man was sentenced to life in prison for the attempted assassination of a presidential candidate for a September 2024 incident at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Fla. Ryan Routh was observed pointing an assault-style rifle behind a fence on the perimeter of the golf course, officials said, as Trump golfed with others hundreds of metres away.

That incident occurred two months after a Pennsylvania man shot at Trump at a campaign stop in Butler, Pa. in July 2024. The gunman and an innocent bystander were killed in the chaotic series of events, in which Trump was bloodied and pumped his fist to the crowd.
