World.title: The longest musical composition in the world changes chords for the first time in two years
World.content:
Certain artists love to defy standard 2-hour runtimes when it comes to concerts, with the likes of Bruce Springsteen and The Cure known for their lengthy and bladder-punishing setlists.

 

However, none can compete with an organ in Germany, which is playing one composition in essentially the world's slowest concert - one which will outlive us all.

Aptly titled 'ORGAN²/ASLSP (As SLow aS Possible)', the piece began playing on 5 September 2001 at the medieval St Burchardi church in the eastern town of Halberstadt in Germany and won't finish until the year 2640.

The organ of the John Cage Organ Project Halberstadt is illuminated prior to a chord change inside the medieval Burchardi Church in Halberstadt, Germany - 5 August 2026 AP Photo

Composed by boundary-pushing avant-garde US composer John Cage, the piece is played so slowly that any chord change in the John Cage Organ Project Halberstadt becomes news and draws thousands of visitors. And today is one of those rare days when a new note is played.

The change - from seven notes to eight once an A4 pipe is added - represents the 17th change and the completion of about 4 per cent of the 639-year endeavour.

The last chord change took place two years ago, on 5 February 2024.

Inside the medieval Burchardi Church in Halberstadt, Germany - Wednesday 5 August 2026 AP Photo

So, how does it work? Put simply, an electric-powered blower system sends wind into the organ to create a continuous sound. Since it's impossible for a musician to hold down the keys for so long, the chord changes - done manually - are also possible with the use of small sandbags to keep the sound going.

Curator Anneli Borgmann, chairwoman of the John Cage Organ Project Halberstadt's board of trustees, lifts a new pipe for a test - 6 July 2026 AP Photo

Originally written for piano in 1985, Cage adapted the piece in an arrangement for organ before he died in 1992. He never specified how long the piece should be played, leaving a single cryptic note: “ASLSP,” meaning “as slowly and softly as possible.”

They took that note seriously and very literally. Still, it's a fitting tribute to a composer who wasn’t afraid of breaking down our understanding of what music can be.

Organ builder Johannes Huefken adjusts a new pipe for a test - 6 July 2026 AP Photo

Mark your calendars: the next chord change is set to take place on 5 October 2027 with the release of the E4 sound – previously added on 5 September 2020.

In case you were struggling in the ideas department for a multi-generational gift, inheritable “final tickets” for the 4 September 2640 event are already being sold. They’ll set you back €2,640. But then again, your future family member will have bragging rights when it comes to being there on the final day (and note) of the longest composition the world has ever heard.

World.title: Ukraine failed to shoot down a single Russian missile launched in overnight barrage
World.content:
Ukraine was unable to shoot down a single Russian missile during an overnight attack that left at least 17 people dead in Kyiv and the surrounding region, according to a daily air force report published on Wednesday.

 

The Russian army sent 115 drones and fired 28 high-speed missiles, including ballistic ones, the air force said, at a time officials have lamented a drastic shortage of anti-ballistic munitions.

President Voloydmyr Zelenskyy confirmed in a post on social media that “the main target of the attack was the warehouses of civilian enterprises, there were also strikes on infrastructure, a railway station."

"Ballistics interceptors are something that could have saved the lives of those who died today. It is very important that partners realise that delays in their delivery or unwillingness to transfer anti-ballistics leads to such terrible victims and destruction," he added.

Firefighters put out a fire after Russian missiles hit a warehouse in Kyiv, 5 August, 2026 AP Photo

The highest number of casualties from the night-time attack by Russian forces in the Kyiv region was recorded near the Kvitneva railway station in the Brovary district.

People did not manage to board the last train, which was delayed, and remained on the platform. Eight people were killed, according to Vitaliy Bigun, head of the Brovary District State Administration.

Ukraine’s Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said that Moscow did not target any military facilities, only civilian sites.

“These strikes have no military purpose – this is terrorism,” he said.

“Russia is expanding its campaign of terror by deliberately targeting businesses that serve millions of people. Ukrainian manufacturers, commercial facilities, and logistics hubs came under attack.”

Ukrainian non-military businesses hit

Koretskyi said the government is setting up a meeting with Ukrainian businesses targeted by Russian strikes.

Key facilities belonging to Epicentre, the county’s leader in the DIY segment, ROZETKA, the largest online retailer and e-commerce marketplaceand Nova Poshta, Ukraine’s largest private postal and courier company have been destroyed.

According to Nova Poshta Russian forces used cluster munitions during the strike on its sorting centre in Kyiv.

Supermarket chain Silpo said six of its employees were killed when fires broke out at two distribution centres.

In a separate air strike on Tuesday, Russian forces destroyed a warehouse complex where products belonging to Ukrainian ice cream manufacturer Lasunka were being stored.

World.title: These are the best ‘dupes’ for travel hot spots like Venice, Lake Como and Kyoto
World.content:
There are certain destinations around the world everyone wants to visit at least once: Venice. Lake Como. Saint-Tropez.

 

But overtourism in many of these top spots is becoming a huge problem, and not everyone has the luxury of being able to travel in shoulder- or off-season to dodge the crowds.

Enter: The “destination dupe”.

You get to experience all the reasons the original city is popular without the crowds, and an under-the-radar destination benefits from tourism cash. Plus, you’re easing the pressure put on places that just don’t want or need any more visitors.

Over the years, we’ve seen some rather dubious dupes (my favourite has to be the “Maldives of Poland”... aka Park Gródek), but the team at eSIM provider Holafly have done their homework on this new ranking.

Each destination pair was evaluated based on its visual and cultural similarity, accommodation savings based on average peak-season hotel prices, visitor pressure, accessibility, and momentum across social media and online search platforms.

All the alternatives offered are in a different country to the original, and there are no more than two substitutes from the same nation.

This is so the ranking “prioritises destinations that deliver a similar experience while providing better value, fewer crowds and the opportunity to discover somewhere new”.

The best travel destination dupes

The best travel dupe? That would be Ghent in Belgium, which replaces Venice. All the medieval canals and historic architecture, without having to battle past crowds for a photo on the Rialto Bridge.

Next up on the ranking was Banff in Canada, which is a dupe for Aspen in the US. Both spots have Rocky Mountains, both have incredible skiing, and you won’t have to pay the kind of prices Aspen’s soaring popularity with the rich and famous have brought.

Third place went to Jeonju in South Korea, which replaced Kyoto in Japan. Japan’s struggles with overtourism are well known, with the country recently increasing its visa fees fivefold in a bid to combat the surge of tourists.

In Jeonju, you’ll be able to explore traditional architecture in the hanok village, visit Gyeonggijeon Shrine, and learn more about the history of the Three Kingdom period at the Jeonju National Museum. For foodies, it’s also the birthplace of bibimbap.

World.title: Iceland orders expulsion and re-entry ban on 21 anti-whaling activists, police say
World.content:
Iceland has ordered the expulsion of 21 anti-whaling activists held in Reykjavik since last week after their ship was seized while pursuing a whaling vessel, police told the AFP news agency on Wednesday.

 

The Bandero, a ship belonging to a foundation led by animal rights activist Paul Watson, was boarded by Icelandic authorities off the island nation's coast after it obstructed the operations of one of Iceland's last remaining whaling ships, the Hvalur 9.

"All crew members of the Bandero have now been served notice of a decision on expulsion and a re-entry ban," police spokesman Gunnar Runar Sveinbjornsson told AFP in an email.

One of those aboard the Bandero told AFP the activists had initially intended to ram the whaling ship but were too slow and instead launched an inflatable boat to deploy a net that would damage the whaling ship's propellers. That also failed.

Icelandic police have accused the activists of "suspected violations of international law of the sea and endangering maritime security" and requested their expulsion and a ban on their return to Iceland.

An Icelandic Coast Guard vessel taken from the protest vessel Bandero, 30 July, 2026 AP Photo

Those aboard the Bandero included Americans, Brazilians, French and Spanish, according to a list provided by the Captain Paul Watson Foundation.

Paul Watson was not on board.

The crew had been confined to the vessel in the Reykjavik port but police said Wednesday they could now leave the ship.

The foundation said their vessel had been in international waters when boarded.

It said the crew's detention was excessive and denounced the seizure of their phones.

Iceland is one of the only countries that still allows commercial whaling. Norway and Japan are the others.

The Icelandic government plans to introduce a bill this autumn aimed at banning the practice.

World.title: My sleep deprivation is your natural short sleep
World.content:
Every so often we hear of high-ranking politicians or CEOs claiming to get by on very little sleep — some as little as three hours a night. If they’re not Natural Short Sleepers, chances are they’re heading for trouble.

I've been having trouble sleeping — for as long as forever. Sometimes it's just a feeling. Other times, it's a fact (I know because my watch tells me). But then my watch may be part of the problem. It's constantly reminding me to get to bed on time and accosting me with poor sleep scores. It drives my anxiety through the roof, my heart races and I feel like I can't sleep. But then I still feel fine the next day. Weird.

"When you're sleep deprived, you have poor judgment," said Catia Reis, a sleep researcher at the University of Lisbon, when we spoke.

That might explain my predicament. Because even when I feel fine during the week, I oversleep at the weekend — which is a sure sign of sleep debt, she said.

Reis has studied a variety of sleep-related conditions, including the effects of jet lag and sleep deprivation among athletes.

One investigation compared levels of sleepiness among patients with sleep apnea — a condition where you stop breathing intermittently through the night — and shift workers, who work against their natural, circadian rhythm. That's our inner clock that tells us when we're wakeful or sleepy.

She compared the results from both subjective assessments made by participants and objective, clinical tests, and found a "mismatch" in people's ability to assess their own levels of sleepiness the more they were exposed to that very thing: sleepiness.

Basically, the brain stops working. And that should be concerning, given that the brain plays a central role in sleep.

Sleep or die

When we sleep, the body performs several restorative functions: It removes toxins we have ingested through food or the atmosphere, generates new energy and is essential for our learning and memory.

"Sleep involves many parts of the brain," said Ying-Hui Fu, a sleep researcher at the University of California San Franscisco. "Almost every disease of the brain, including neurological and psychiatric, [can be linked to] sleep problems."

On average, people need about 7.5-8.5 hours' sleep per night.

But every so often we hear about people in demanding jobs, usually politicians, boasting — or claiming credibility — by saying they rarely sleep more than a few hours; like they're ALWAYS WORKING FOR THE PEOPLE.

Most recently, it was Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who reminded us she's slept between zero and three hours per night while in office.

As a former heavy metal drummer, you might expect a certain level of stamina from the Japanese PM. But while voluntary, habitual (or trained) sleep deprivation — if that's what it is in Takaichi's case — may be an impressive sleep-work-no-life-balance ethic, it's not a good, long-term strategy.

In the best-case scenario, a long-term "sleep debt" can cause your body to accumulate toxins, risking heart or brain disease. In the worst-case scenario, it can be fatal.

Why sleep is so important for your immune system To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"There are only two things more important than sleep for our total health," Fu told DW. "One is air. If we don't have air, we die in a few minutes. The other is water. If we don't have water, we die in a few days. If you don't eat, you can live a couple of months. But if you don't sleep, you can probably only live for a couple of weeks."

And that goes for all animals — "if we don't sleep, we die," she said.

The exception: natural short sleepers

Natural short sleepers are the exception to the rule. They can sleep fewer than six hours per night and not only feel fine, but also actually are fine — healthy, happy and energetic. They appear to have genetic variations that allow them to thrive. Fu cited an 80-year-old Natural Short Sleeper who competed in triathlons.

Fu and her lab found the first of these variations in the gene DEC2 and published their findings in 2009. Ten years later, they published a paper suggesting that the gene ADRB1 was also linked to Natural Short Sleeper Syndrome. Findings into the genes NPSR1, GRM1, SIK3 followed, and there are others in the pipeline.

We're calling them gene "variations" rather than "mutations" because mutations are often associated with negative health effects. But it appears that Natural Short Sleep does not risk the health issues that habitual short sleepers or sleep deprived people face.

The genes show a range of functions that sleep effects:

DEC2: helps regulate sleep/wake duration

ADRB1: mediates cardiac and neuronal signaling

NPSR1: helps modulate arousal and anxiety

GRM1: involved in brain function; may be linked to depression

SIK3: plays a role in cell cycle-, metabolic and inflammatory- regulation

Each has taken years of painstaking basic — foundational — research to find and test.

"Every one of us has between 500 to 1,000 unique mutations in our genome. To know which one is causal is very difficult," said Fu.

Sleep smarter: How your body clock shapes your health To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The impact of better sleep on humanity

The number of known Natural Short Sleepers is small, but Fu says Short Sleeper Syndrome is likely to be more common than research currently suggests.

Most of Fu's findings are limited families that share a gene variation. That's been for a practical, methodological reason: If three members of a family have the same variation and they all appear to be healthy on only four to six hours' sleep, then that gene variation may well be responsible, especially if it's in a gene that is known to be important for healthy sleep function. But it's early days.

"We just know that they perform better and they're healthier. And the most logical explanation for me is that their sleep function is better," said Fu.

Reis is also cautious about the state of research in this area, saying there are still too few studies into Natural Short Sleepers.

"When objectively test [Habitual Short Sleepers] and we expand their sleep, we know they improve," said Reis. "But the problem is we don't have enough longitudinal studies with [Natural Short Sleepers]."

Fu would agree. But she said it was a struggle to get the research financed.

"My goal is to help everybody get good sleep. Because if we can help everybody get good sleep, all diseases will drop," said Fu. "The entire spectrum of disease incidence would drop. Can you imagine the impact on humanity?"

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Nepal province legalizes use of medical marijuana
World.content:
A provincial government in Nepal has legalized the use and growing of marijuana for medical purposes despite a national ban.

A controversial bill allowing the cultivation and medical use of cannabis, which was endorsed by the chief of Nepal's Gandaki province, took effect on Monday.

However, farmers will required to obtain official permission from the provincial authorities and will be subject to close monitoring.

According to Kathmandu Post, province assembly members from the ruling coalition and opposition parties unanimously passed the legislation.

Gandaki is one of Nepal's seven provinces. The province is home to some of the country's most popular mountains and hiking trails, as well as the resort city of Pokhara.

Marijuana outlawed in Nepal

Gandaki's provincial law sets a precedent in Nepal because it was passed despite a national ban on the cultivation, possession, and use of marijuana.

Possession of marijuana for personal use can result in a one-month jail sentence, while its distribution and sale are punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment, depending on the amount involved.

However, cannabis is native to Nepal, where it is widely used during festivals. Activists have long been campaigning for the government to change the law to permit its cultivation and use.

Marijuana was once deeply embedded in the country's culture and religious traditions. However, in the late 1970s, Nepal joined other nations in outlawing marijuana and expelling the hippies who had flocked there.

World.title: Fact check: Did misleading claims about Spain's migration law trigger the Ceuta crisis?
World.content:
More than 70 people died after thousands of migrants tried to cross from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. The crossings have been linked to misleading claims about a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling.

Misleading social media posts appear to have contributed to a sudden surge in migrant crossings into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta. Tens of thousands of people attempted to cross from Morocco in late July. According to authorities, dozens drowned or were killed in crowd-related incidents during the crossings, which triggered a major humanitarian crisis.

European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities blamed the sudden surge in crossings on incorrect information circulating on social media and human traffickers. A recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling on migrant returns became the focus of many of the misleading claims.

The decision was issued several weeks earlier . It ruled that migrants who arrive by sea cannot be subject to the same fast-track deportation procedure applied to people intercepted while crossing physical border infrastructure, such as fences and other official barriers.

Posts on social media claimed that the ruling effectively prevented Spanish authorities from returning migrants who reached Spanish territory by sea, implying that they would be allowed to remain in the country.

The ruling was widely misrepresented online. DW Fact check examined how the claims spread and what the court actually decided.

What was circulating on social media?

Claim: "The Spanish Supreme Court issued a ruling considered one of the most prominent decisions in the migration file, prohibiting the immediate deportation of irregular migrants..."

The claim appeared in Arabic in a Facebook post published on July 13, which described the ruling as "historic." It was one of dozens of similar posts reviewed by DW Fact Check. Some of the accounts spreading the claim were linked to migration-focused pages active on platforms including Telegram, where one profile promoted information about migration opportunities abroad under the slogan "All opportunities for immigration abroad are in your hands."

DW Fact Check also identified numerous examples of smaller and medium-sized accounts sharing posts that used identical or nearly identical wording to the version cited in this article.

One of the misleading posts claiming that a Spanish Supreme Court ruling prevents the deportation of irregular migrants Image: facebook

DW Fact check: Misleading.

The ruling applies only to migrants arriving by sea who have not crossed a border barrier on their way; it does not apply to all migrants.

Under Spanish law , authorities may carry out immediate returns of people intercepted while breaching official border infrastructure. Migrants who arrive by sea are in a different legal situation because they haven't crossed a barrier. Their cases must be processed individually, with the procedural guarantees the law requires.

The ruling therefore limits the use of immediate returns in these specific cases, but it does not grant migrants an automatic right to remain in Spain. It also allows the government to install physical barriers at sea, which Spain has since done to close what many described as a legal loophole .

Many of the posts reviewed by DW Fact check quoted the ruling without explaining its legal scope. In one example, a TikTok user said “...this law that came out in Spain says it is forbidden to send anyone back if they came swimming to Spain, and it is forbidden for the navy to send them back. This is true...”

The video presented the ruling as a general prohibition on returning migrants who arrive by sea. It did not mention that the Supreme Court’s decision involved the legal procedure for carrying out returns, not a blanket ban on deportation.

DW Fact Check found that this selective interpretation — highlighting the restriction on immediate returns while omitting the broader legal context — appeared repeatedly across a large share of the accounts reviewed.

Alone in Ceuta, 15-year-old Moroccan teen faces uncertainty To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can misleading social media claims alone explain the movement toward Ceuta?

The causes of the surge in migrant crossings quickly became the subject of a political dispute between Spain and Morocco.

Spanish officials, including Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, said on July 31 that organized networks had exploited the situation by spreading inaccurate information about the Supreme Court ruling. Madrid also criticized Morocco for failing to prevent thousands of people from reaching the border with Ceuta.

Moroccan authorities rejected accusations that they had deliberately allowed the crossings to happen and said that misleading information on social media caused the mass movement.

According to Lorenzo Piccoli, Assistant Professor of Migration Governance at the European University Institute, the Supreme Court ruling may have played a role in encouraging some people to attempt the crossing, but it could not explain a movement of this scale on its own.

"Even in 2015 and 2016, when up to a million people arrived in Europe, we never saw more than 5,000 or 6,000 in a single day. Here we are talking about 50,000 to 60,000 in one day," Piccoli told DW.

He said it would have been "very difficult" for online claims alone to trigger such a large-scale movement in such a short period of time. "It's very hard to see how this would have happened without some form of coordination or without authorities allowing it to happen," he said.

Piccoli added that there appeared to be a broader political dimension to the crisis, with Morocco potentially not actively causing the movement but failing to prevent it. "There is a recognition that perhaps the Moroccan government did not actively provoke this event, but in some ways it did nothing to avoid it from happening," he said.

World.title: Hungary's Lake Velence is drying up
World.content:
Hungary is feeling the heat. The country's third-largest lake is shrinking, the Danube is running low, and soaring temperatures could force the country's only nuclear power plant to shut down.

A dead fish lies half-decayed on the shore. Its eyes have been picked out by the birds.

Hungary's Lake Velence will likely experience a massive fish kill. That's because oxygen levels in the body of water are too low, according to environmental experts. This means more and more fish will suffocate.

Hungary has seen temperatures soar to 40 degrees Celsius, with barely any rain. This heat is having a major impact on the country's third-largest natural lake.

Its water has never been particularly deep, but the current situation is dire. Water levels have been recorded in Agard, on the southern shore, since 1933. It dropped to a historic low in September 2022, measuring just 53 centimeters. Yet as of today, August 4, the water level has dropped to a mere 29 centimeters (11 inches).

As long as it doesn't rain and temperatures remain hot, the water level will continue to drop every day, by half a centimeter per day on average. The water is currently evaporating at such a fast pace that there may soon be no continuous body of water left, only isolated pools. This could mark a critical tipping point for the lake.

The impact of Hungary's ongoing drought is already clearly visible. The lake has receded by dozens of meters. Ground once covered in water is now so dry that the soil is cracking. The reed belt surrounding the lake, which serves as a habitat for numerous bird species, is now largely rooted in dry soil.

But not all living creatures are suffering under the current conditions: that's evident from a constant hum in the air near the water's edge. As fish and aquatic plants find their habitats shrinking, flies, bacteria, and other decomposers take over, breaking down what the drought leaves behind.

No swimming

The water shortage isn't just changing the lake — it's changing the entire region. Lake Velence is a popular tourist destination, located just 50 kilometers from Hungary's capital, Budapest. It is considered less crowded than nearby Lake Balaton.

Swimming is not an option this summer at Lake Velence Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

But these days, there are barely any visitors. The remaining water has turned a brownish-green and taken on a slightly musty odor. A "No Swimming" sign has been put up, with yellow tape blocking access to the water. Five swimming spots have been closed to the public since July 23.

The Velence municipal government says the beach will only reopen once the lake's water quality improves, though it is unclear when that might happen. The persistent heat and low water levels mean the lake's water is getting warmer and warmer, leading to a growth in bacteria and blue-green algae.

Tourist industry under pressure

The people living around the lake, who make their living in the region's tourist sector, are hard hit by the lake's falling water levels. Today, only one family is visiting the northern beach — not for swimming but sunbathing. There is a water slide, slowly rusting away, with the end of the chute not even reaching the water anymore.

Only one kiosk is open today. A woman is selling langos, Hungary's well-known fried bread, as well as ice cream and lemonade. "The slide hasn't been used for years," the saleswoman tells DW. "It really needs fixing, but who will pay for it when fewer and fewer tourists come here?" Campsites and holiday homes around the lake seem deserted, with many stores closed.

Peggy Barath works in an ice cream shop on Velence Promenade, telling DW, "We've always had a lot of tourists here." She says many visitors were from East Germany, the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. But in recent years, their numbers have been dwindling "because of the lake's low water levels."

Peggy Barath hopes the situation will improve and tourists will return Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

Peggy says that the ice cream shop now focuses on cyclists rather than tourists looking to swim, as cyclists are undeterred by low water levels.

No long-term solution in sight

Major interventions in the region's water cycle have made the lake more vulnerable to droughts over the years. "The lakeshore has been subject to significant construction activity over the past 15 years," Zoltan Kun, president of the Hungarian Great Lakes and Wetlands Association, tells DW.

"The water management authority has focused on quickly draining excess water from the region rather than storing it using nature-based solutions. And the agricultural industry destroyed our soils, which means they are less able to absorb water."

This isn't the first time Lake Velence has dried up. When this happened in the early 1990s, the lake was replenished with water from various other sources, a solution that proved effective but also expensive and time-consuming. That's why experts are calling for a more sustainable solution today, especially since climate change means more drought periods are expected.

The Zamolyi and Patkai reservoirs could, for instance, be renovated so that water could be stored there during periods of heavy rainfall. During dry spells, this water could then be diverted into Lake Valance.

The dry, cracked bed of Hungary's third-largest lake Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

Yet little has happened so far. In 2021, the government at the time, led by Prime Minister Viktor Orban, rejected a broad investment program for the lake on the grounds that it was too costly. Other projects, however, went ahead.

A new canoe center

Although it has long been clear that water levels drop to a critical level in summer and fall, authorities built a brand-new canoeing center on the north shore between 2021 and 2024, suitable for international competitions. The project cost about 140 million euros in government funds.

Lanes are marked off in the lake with buoys in front of the newly built spectator tower. It's very quiet, like elsewhere along the body of water. Floating docks sit low in the greenish-brown water.

The World University Canoe Championships were supposed to be held here in August, the first major event to be staged at the newly built center. Yet due to persistently low water levels, the event was moved to Szeged, southern Hungary, instead.

This means that for the time being, the Lake Velence facility remains nothing more than an expensive training center.

A sandbank has formed in front of Budapest's Margaret Island Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW

Nuclear power plant on brink of shutdown

Hungary's ongoing heat wave is being felt all over the country. Water levels of the Danube River have dropped significantly, exposing stretches of dry riverbed around Budapest's Margaret Island. Tourists and locals alike are taking in the unusual sight, snapping photos on a sandbar that has emerged off the island. The low water level has also attracted scrap-metal collectors, who use magnets to pull rusty metal objects from parts of the river that are normally submerged.

The low water level has dramatic consequences. With the exception of a few sightseeing steamboats, boat traffic has almost ceased on the Danube River. Not only that. Paks nuclear power plant, located about 100 kilometers downstream from Budapest, can no longer be cooled with Danube water. The site's electricity output, which covers about half of Hungary's power consumption, has been gradually reduced over the past few days, and it is set to be shut down later this week for the first time ever.

Hungary's power options after drought shuts nuclear plant To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We are facing a crisis that is beyond our control and putting us to the test," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said at a joint press conference with Interim President Agnes Forsthoffer on Monday. He added that the next five days would be the most critical of the summer of 2026.

Magyar has asked the Hungarian public to conserve electricity. Many companies have agreed to voluntarily reduce their power consumption. Some public buildings and bridges are no longer illuminated at night, and rail freight traffic is suspended between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m.

Hungary faces a very challenging time, with temperatures over 40 degrees Celsius expected over the next days.

This article was translated from German

World.title: TikTok influencer shot dead during livestream in Mexico
World.content:
Cesar Gastelum, a Mexican influencer with nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok, was shot dead in the middle of a livestream.

Mexican social media influencer Cesar Gastelum was shot and killed on Tuesday while livestreaming with friends outside a fast food restaurant in Culiacan, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, local authorities said.

Gastelum, who had close to 600,000 followers on TikTok, was known for comedy content. He was broadcasting live outside the restaurant with two friends, all reportedly dressed as delivery drivers as part of a challenge for the video.

What do we know?

During the stream, a motorcycle carrying two people pulled up beside them. Footage from the livestream appeared to show the motorcycle driver shooting at Gastelum's head directly. The broadcast cut out at that moment.

While the video was later taken down by the platform, portions of it continuted to circulate online.

A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastelum's death and said a major security operation was under way. Local television footage showed soldiers and police at the scene, a busy commercial plaza near the state prosecutor's office in Culiacan, while forensic investigators collected evidence.

Initial police reports described the victim as a delivery worker. He was later identified as Gastelum, who local media reported was around 25 years old, after the video and witness accounts helped confirm his identity.

We met a cartel killer — who really runs Mexico? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Culiacan at the center of a conflict between rival crime factions

Culiacan, the capital of Sinaloa, has been gripped by violence for the past two years amid an internal power struggle within the region's dominant drug cartel. Local press have reported that several influencers, some allegedly linked to criminal groups, have been killed in Sinaloa in recent years.

The killing echoes the May 2025 death of beauty influencer Valeria Marquez, 23, who was shot while livestreaming on TikTok at the salon where she worked in Zapopan, in Mexico’s western state of Jalisco. Her death was investigated as possible femicide.

Local authorities arrested Ramon Angel Alvarez Ayala, also known as "El R-1," in Jalisco in July. Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch described him as the head of a criminal cell tied to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). Investigators say Alvarez Ayala played a role in Marquez's death and that he financed and directed the November 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo.

World.title: Low water levels in the Danube revealing Nazi shipwrecks
World.content:
There are believed to be about 200 Nazi ships on the floor of the Danube near Prahovo, Serbia. Ferries, tourist boats, and shipping have also become severely restricted due to the drought.

Europe's second-longest river, the Danube, has reached levels so low that sunken German battleships from World War II have emerged from the dried-out riverbed.

Near Prahovo, a Serbian port where the Danube separates the country from Romania, a rusty hull and broken mast has become visible where the Nazis once purposely sunk their own ship to avoid capture by the Russians.

Both the Rhine and the Danube have seen World War II-era ships appear due to low water levels Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

The Serbian government has long sought help from the European Union to remove what are believed to be hundreds of ships, some still laden with weapons, from the river floor. But pinpointing their exact locations without accidentally disturbing the explosives still onboard has been an issue.

Low water levels in the Danube have pushed some power plants in parts of Central and Eastern Europe to the brink of shutting down.

The Danube flows through ten countries, including Germany and Austria Image: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS

Ferries, tourism boats, and shipping on both the Danube and the Rhine river have been drastically reduced in recent weeks due to the drought.

In recent years, climate change has made lower water levels in Europe's key waterways a recurring issue.

Tne Nazis sunk hundreds of ships in the Danube to ward off a Soviet advance in 1944 Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: Germany news: Lightning strike cuts Bavarian town in two
World.content:
08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell

A court in Hamburg has handed down prison sentences of up to five years to eight alleged members and supporters of the far-right group "Letzte Verteidigungswelle" (Last Line of Defense).

The Higher Regional Court convicted the young defendants on charges including membership in a terrorist organization and attempted murder.

Prosecutors said the group had planned bomb and arson attacks targeting refugees and left-wing activists and had already carried out several attacks.

Seven defendants received juvenile prison sentences ranging from two years and four months to five years. Another was given an 18-month suspended sentence. Three defendants were also convicted of leading the group.

The presiding judge said they had aimed to "create chaos."

Authorities dismantled the group in May last year after investigations spanning several German states.

Prosecutors said members carried out an overnight arson attack on an occupied cultural center in Altdöbern in October 2024 and a pyrotechnic attack on a refugee accommodation center in Schmölln, Thuringia, in January 2025.

No one was injured, although investigators said that was partly down to chance.

The group had also been planning another attack on a refugee center in Senftenberg, Brandenburg.

Several suspects were arrested in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg and Hesse. They were between 14 and 21 years old at the time.

Because some defendants were minors, much of the trial was held behind closed doors. The verdict was delivered publicly.

World.title: South Korea: Police raid Starbucks HQ over 'Tank Day' fiasco
World.content:
Starbucks Korea faced major backlash after being accused of trivializing a 1980 massacre. Police say their internal investigation was not thorough enough.

Police raided Starbucks' nation headquarters in South Korea on Wednesday, the company confirmed, after a controversial promotional event led to large protests and boycotts of the coffee chain across the country.

"The Seoul police raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea this morning as part of the ongoing investigation," said a spokesman for the Shinsegae Group, which operates Starbucks Korea.

What was the controversial promotion?

This past May, Starbucks advertised large to-go cups they called "tank tumblers" and seemed to refer to the Gwangju Uprising as "tank day."

On May 18, 1980, the ruling military junta violently put down a pro-democracy protest in the city of Gwangju. At least 165 civilians were killed when the army rolled tanks out into the streets to quell the demonstation.

The Starbucks promotional event also appeared to allude to statements made by the government at the time to deny that they had tortured a student protest leader to death.

The backlash was swift, and led to protest and boycotts against the coffee giant in what is the company's third-largest market after the United States and China.

President Lee Jae Myung also expressed his outrage, and Shinsegae Group chairman Chung Yong-jin and Starbucks Korea CEO Son Jung-hyun resigned following a public apology.

What are police investigating?

Starbucks Korea said it conducted its own internal investigation into the matter and found no evidence of wrongdoing. However, the firm admitted that the inquiry had been hampered by, amongst other things, not being able to compel the people involved in planning the promotion to hand over their phones.

Police told the Yonhap news agency they were looking for evidence that executives knowingly trivialized the 1980 massacre.

World.title: La Audiencia Nacional pregunta a la Guardia Civil si tuvo alguna información que pudiese “alertar” de la entrada masiva en Ceuta
World.content:
La entrada irregular de más de 70.000 personas en Ceuta desde Marruecos, producida fundamentalmente el pasado jueves, comienza a judicializarse. La Audiencia Nacional ha solicitado a la Guardia Civil que informe de si tuvo algún indicio o información, los días previos a la avalancha, que alertase de que esta se iba a producir. La investigación se inició a raíz de una denuncia del partido Iustitia Europa en la que pedía al tribunal que investigase los delitos “contra la seguridad del Estado, delitos contra la Nación, favorecimiento de la inmigración ilegal y tráfico de personas, organización criminal y omisión del deber de perseguir delitos”.

La cuestión de si hubo indicios o alertas previas que pudiesen haber preparado a los efectivos situados en la frontera, que fueron completamente superados por la avalancha humana, es una de las claves de esta crisis. El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, insistía este miércoles en que el Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) no alertó de una llegada masiva de migrantes a Ceuta. Pero sí admitía que hubo avisos en los días previos de que, como es habitual en verano, podía haber “una ampliación, una elevación” del número de entradas irregulares por mar en la ciudad autónoma y de que en esta ocasión se podían “ver fomentadas” por la sentencia del Tribunal Supremo de comienzos de julio que prohibía las devoluciones en caliente de aquellas personas que entrasen a nado.

En una providencia a la que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, la magistrada titular del Tribunal Central de Instancia número 3, María Tardón, solicita además a la Jefatura de Información del instituto armado que dé detalles sobre los días más críticos de la crisis migratoria —el 30 y el 31 de julio—, “particularmente en lo relativo a las operaciones de rescate de las personas que se hayan localizado en las aguas territoriales españolas, sus circunstancias personales conocidas, así como, en el caso de personas fallecidas, si constara la causa y la data de la muerte y, en el caso de las personas supervivientes, su identidad y datos de localización”.

Más información Playa de Trampolín: el refugio a sol abierto para centenares de subsaharianos que resisten en busca de asilo

El balance provisional de fallecidos es de 77. En las primeras horas, tras la entrada irregular de más de 70.000 personas del jueves, se recuperaron del mar 20 cuerpos. Al día siguiente fueron unos 40. Sus cuerpos se custodian ahora en un hangar refrigerado en el viejo hospital militar de la ciudad autónoma. Las autopsias casi están terminadas y se buscan formas de colaboración con Marruecos para identificar a los fallecidos.

No es la primera decisión de la instructora dentro de esta, de momento, incipiente causa: este martes, la magistrada solicitó a la Policía Nacional un informe sobre la entrada “irregular masiva” de migrantes en Ceuta en los últimos días para dilucidar si se trató de “una acción concertada o dirigida” por algún “grupo criminal”. La solicitud busca establecer si la Audiencia Nacional es competente para investigar y más tarde juzgar los delitos denunciados por Iustitia Europa, partido que forma parte de las acusaciones populares de, entre otros, el juicio al hermano de Pedro Sánchez o de la causa contra la esposa del presidente del Gobierno, Begoña Gómez.

World.title: Penélope Cruz y Salma Hayek: la anécdota del maquillaje como prueba de una de las amistades más sólidas de Hollywood
World.content:
La española ha comentado que una entrevista reciente que su amistad es tan cercana que incluso la ha peinado y maquillado cuando ha fallado el equipo de Salma. Un ‘brochazo’ más sobre una amistad de más de 20 años

Cuando, en una entrevista para la revista Allure, Olivia Wilde preguntó a Penélope Cruz por algún secreto de belleza hollywoodiense, la de Alcobendas explicó que, hace años, su amiga Salma Hayek la llamó para pedirle un inmenso favor. “Tengo un estreno y necesito que me peines y me maquilles. Por cierto, se ha ido la luz en casa, así que no tenemos electricidad y mi equipo de peluquería y maquillaje me ha cancelado”, le dijo la mexicana. Como la madre de Cruz, Encarna Sánchez, regentaba una peluquería en Alcobendas, el reto no le pareció inverosímil tras haber crecido rodeada de secadores y, tras encender unas velas, maquilló y peinó a su amiga, que acudió al estreno de Dogma luciendo espectacular.

Aunque, por descontado, la anécdota es carne de ‘salseo’ hollywoodiense, en realidad no es nada extraño que, más allá de la meca del cine, las mujeres se ayuden a la hora de arreglarse y encuentren en las sesiones de maquillaje compartidas un espacio de sororidad y unión. La maquilladora Maite Tuset así lo confirma: “Maquillarse tiene una parte muy bonita: compartir. Entre amigas es muy habitual ayudarnos, recomendarnos productos, probar técnicas nuevas y disfrutar juntas de ese momento. Lo que no sabe una lo sabe la otra”, explica a S Moda.

Penélope Cruz y Salma Hayek en la Gala amfAR contra el sida. Toni Anne Barson Archive (WireImage)

Una amistad ‘made in Hollywood’

La amistad entre Hayek y Cruz no se ha construido únicamente a base de eyeliners y moldeados, sino también de alfombras rojas, rodajes, colchones compartidos y premios. El comienzo de su relación amistosa fue fruto de la admiración. Así lo explicó la mexicana en Vogue Arabia, donde fue la propia Penélope la encargada de entrevistar a su amiga. “La prensa española me preguntó con quién me gustaría trabajar y contesté que con Penélope Cruz. Empezamos a hablar y tú tenías que venir a Los Ángeles para hacer audiciones y conocer a representantes. Era al comienzo de nuestras carreras y te dije: “¿Por qué no te quedas en mi casa? Puedo ir a recogerte al aeropuerto”. Fui a recogerte y recuerdo que, la primera vez que nos vimos, ambas sonreímos. Y después vinieron más de veinte años de sólida amistad. Fue una conexión inmediata, como si nos conociéramos de toda la vida”.

Cuando Salma Hayek acudió a Madrid para recoger el Premio al Personaje del Año de Vanity Fair en 2018, Cruz fue su acompañante y la encargada de pronunciar el discurso con el que fue homenajeada. Tras recordar la forma en la que se conocieron, añadió: “Salma es de esas personas que, cuando las conoces, no quieres que desaparezcan de tu vida”. Ambas hablan habitualmente la una de la otra como ‘hermana’.

Penélope Cruz, Javier Bardem y Salma Hayek en una imagen de 2005. J. Vespa (WireImage)

En 2024, Cruz volvió a acompañar a su amiga a una entrega de premios. Se trataba de los galardones Innovator del Wall Street Journal, donde la actriz mexicana recogió el premio de manos de Linda Evangelista. Penélope Cruz, que posó con ella cogida de la mano, la observaba desde su mesa con evidente orgullo.

Cuando Penélope llegó a Los Ángeles a finales de los años noventa, a mucha gente le costaba comprender cómo dos actrices latinas que competían por los mismos papeles podían ser tan amigas. En la actualidad, la industria hollywoodiense sigue ofreciendo pocos papeles para las mujeres latinas, pero por aquel entonces parecía que solo había una actriz destinada a interpretar ese tipo de personajes. “A la gente le costaba entender cómo dos mujeres que parecían competir podían tener una relación tan cercana. Y todavía la tenemos. Nunca nos hemos mentido la una a la otra; siempre nos hemos contado en qué estamos trabajando”, aseguró Hayek a Vogue Arabia. “Nos decíamos: ‘Vale, las dos queremos conseguir un papel en esta película, pero si yo no lo logro, espero que tú sí’. Eso nos ayudó a navegar entre la hipocresía y la falsedad de Hollywood. Había algunos proyectos que tú ansiabas más que yo y otros que me interesaban más a mí, y siempre fuimos capaces de hablarlo. Y siempre te llamo cuando quiero trabajar un personaje porque no hay nadie en el mundo que me entienda mejor’, le dijo la actriz a Penélope Cruz.

Penélope Cruz y Salma Hayek en Los Ángeles en 2006. Jesse Grant (WireImage)

Ambas compartieron cartel en el wéstern de acción Bandidas en 2006. “Yo había oído hablar tanto de la rivalidad y de las zancadillas de Hollywood que la actitud de Salma fue una grata sorpresa”, ha asegurado Cruz. Cuando rodaron la película, tenían un ritmo de vida muy diferente al actual, lo que dio pie a un curioso apodo. “Nos llamamos ‘huevos’. Surgió porque, cuando trabajábamos juntas, aún no teníamos hijos, así que dormíamos mucho más que ahora. Era una forma de llamarnos perezosas”, explicó Cruz a la revista Allure. “Dormimos en la misma cama muchísimas veces y ella siempre intentaba despertarme llamándome ‘huevos”, añadió.

Salma Hayek y Penélope Cruz han recorrido juntas la alfombra roja de los Oscar en numerosas ocasiones. Hayek también estuvo presente cuando, en 2000, Cruz le entregó el Oscar a Pedro Almodóvar por Todo sobre mi madre. Años más tarde, Hayek volvió a acompañarla cuando recogió el Oscar por Vicky Cristina Barcelona.

Pedro Almodóvar junto a Cecilia Roth, Penélope Cruz y Salma Hayek el día que ganó el Oscar por 'Todo sobre mi madre'. LUCY NICHOLSON (AFP via Getty Images)

Además de aplausos y piropos, su relación se compone de risas. Penélope Cruz se alió con Ashton Kutcher para hacer una broma a su amiga en el programa Punk’d. Ambas acudieron a cenar al restaurante Geisha House cuando Cruz llevó a Salma a los baños para mostrarle el lamentable estado de uno de los retretes, absolutamente obstruido. Cuando intentaron tirar de la cadena, el váter se desbordó e inundó el aseo. Tras regresar a la mesa, el encargado del local se acercó para quejarse de su comportamiento, mientras otros comensales tachaban a Salma de ‘asquerosa’. Finalmente, Kutcher apareció para explicar que todo había sido una broma. Prueba de que no le guarda rencor es que al responder para una revista a algunas de las preguntas que los internautas hacen más habitualmente sobre ella, cuando descubrió que era común que la gente preguntara si son hermanas, respondió: “Aunque no compartimos sangre, es para mí una hermana”. Una hermana que le acompaña en los momentos más importantes de su vida profesional y personal, que la admira y que incluso le ayuda a estar perfecta en un estreno cuando su equipo de peluquería y maquillaje le fallan.

Penélope Cruz y Salma Hayek en un restaurante de Los Ángeles en 2004. Steve Kondiles/Bauer-Griffin (GC Images)

Las amigas o "hermanas" como ellas se llaman en París en 2006. Marc Ausset-Lacroix (WireImage)

Salma Hayek, John Galliano y Penélope Cruz en Los Ángeles. J. Vespa (WireImage)

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: Glasshouses feel cost of drought as sprinkler ban imposed
World.content:
Glasshouse operators in the Westland region could lose tens of millions of euros after a ban on sprinklers comes into force on Wednesday.

The glasshouse industry has not been exempted from the ban, which has been imposed by the Delfland water authority as an anti-drought measure.

All sluice gates in the region have been closed to protect drinking water from being contaminated by saltwater from the sea. Inspectors will check if companies are complying with the ban on using water for sprinkling.

“These measures are urgently needed to prevent irreversible damage happening,” a spokesman for the water board told Omroep West. “The glasshouse owners have been given until midnight [on Tuesday] to fill their reservoirs.”

Glastuinbouw Nederland, which represents the industry, said a two to three-week ban would cost companies around €150 million.

It has asked the water board if companies can spray their crops with purified waste water or seawater. “Almost any water is better than no water,” a spokesman said.

A ban on drawing water is also in force in parts of the Brabantse Delta region, around Breda. The ban, which initially covered the hours from 9am to 9pm, was extended last week to 24 hours and include fruit growers, who were previously exempt.

On the island of Terschelling, off the coast of Friesland, sheep have been banned from grazing and inspections of dykes have been stepped up amid concerns that the drought is causing cracks to appear.

World.title: Two women die trying to help a child in the sea at Callantsoog
World.content:
Two women died after going into the sea to help a child in trouble off Callantsoog in Noord-Holland on Tuesday afternoon.

A 39-year-old British woman, who had been missing overnight, was found dead on the beach at Groote Keeten, north of where the group ran into difficulty. A 26-year-old woman from Gelderland died on Tuesday after being pulled from the water and given CPR.

The two women went to the aid of a child who was at risk of drowning at about 4.30pm and then got into trouble themselves, broadcaster NOS reported. The child and another swimmer were brought ashore by the lifeguard service and taken to hospital for checks.

The alarm was raised at the Voordijk beach entrance, between Callantsoog and Groote Keeten. Four KNRM lifeboat stations took part in the search alongside the lifeguard service, the coastguard and police, using boats and helicopters from surrounding areas.

The search was called off shortly after 9pm on Tuesday because of the tide and resumed on Wednesday morning.

Police are not investigating the circumstances further, regional broadcaster NH reported. Neither woman has been named.

World.title: Belgium and Netherlands open new high-voltage power line
World.content:
The Netherlands and Belgium have opened a new high-voltage power line that will allow 30% more electricity to flow between the two countries.

The so-called Brabo III project connects Antwerp’s harbour to the Rilland high-voltage station across the border in Zeeland. The scheme is designed to reduce strain on the electricity grid and reduce electricity prices in both countries.

Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten and his Belgian counterpart Bart de Wever both attended the official opening in Antwerp. Jetten said the link was an important step towards ensuring European countries can produce their own energy.

“In recent years that has rapidly become a security issue,” he said. “It might not be how the Brabo III project started, but in today’s world it is an important element.”

De Wever said the line, which will supply power to companies such as BASF and Ineos, was “a new artery for our industry”.

Belgian grid operator Elia has spent 10 years building the power line, including two 192 metre-high masts at the Kallosluis, which links the Schelde to the Waaslandkanaal.

The Netherlands will be able to export up to 30% more solar and wind energy on high production days, while at other times it can import more power to meet rapidly increasing demand.

Utrecht has currently frozen all new applications for high-voltage electricity connections because the network has reached saturation point, while operator Tennet warned earlier in the year that some areas were approaching maximum capacity.

World.title: Bomb disposal experts called in at Limburg wildfire
World.content:
The wildfire near Venray in northern Limburg is under control, but efforts to fight the blaze are being hampered by the presence of unexploded munitions in the ground in an area that experienced heavy fighting at the end of the Second World War, the Limburg-Noord safety authority told broadcaster NOS.

Something that may be an unexploded shell was spotted in the Boschhuizerbergen nature reserve on Tuesday and experts from the defence ministry’s bomb disposal unit were called in. Heavy fighting took place around Venray during the war.

Explosions have been heard in the area over the past two days, but a fire service spokesman told NOS it is not certain these came from munitions. Intense heat can turn resin and moisture inside trees to steam, bursting the wood with a bang.

Keeping crews back from the buried ordnance is not slowing the operation down, the safety authority said, because the heat in those parts of the reserve would be unbearable either way.

Days of work ahead

“The fire stayed stable overnight,” Erik Thijssen of the safety authority told NOS on Wednesday morning. “There was no further spread.” He said the all-clear had not been given but the situation was “stable and manageable”.

Thijssen said putting the fire out completely would take several more days.

An emergency ordinance issued by the mayor of Venray on Tuesday afternoon remains in force. It bars people from entering the area and from flying drones over it.

Helicopters and crews

Defence ministry Chinook helicopters are due back in the air between 10am and 11am, the local safety authority told regional broadcaster L1 Nieuws.

The helicopters had dropped almost 900,000 litres of water on the fire by Tuesday evening, drawn from the Maas in buckets holding 7,600 litres.

Around 100 hectares have burned. The fire is being held inside “stop lines” – a railway line, an asphalt road and wide forest tracks – and firefighters are being rotated in from North Brabant, Utrecht, Drenthe and Friesland.

A fourth teenager has been arrested by police investigating a suspected terror plot, the Dutch prosecution service has said.

The 18-year-old was arrested at his home in Kesteren, Gelderland, on Friday evening by a police special intervention team (DSI) acting on information from the intelligence agency AIVD.

A magistrate in Rotterdam ordered him to be detained in custody for the next 14 days. His contact is restricted with his lawyer.

No weapons were found at his home and prosecutors said there were no signs an attack was imminent.

“At this point in the investigation we have not identified a clear target or moment for an attack,” the prosecution service (Openbare Ministerie) said in a statement.

Last week three youths aged 16, 17 and 19 were arrested in overnight raids at homes in Rotterdam, Alkmaar and Eindhoven.

The eldest suspect, named as Mohammed K., was convicted two years ago of planning attacks on nightclubs and police stations in Belgium, none of which took place.

The other two were among a group of 14 people aged between 14 and 30 who were arrested last April on suspicion of inciting terrorism via the social media platform TikTok.

World.title: Dutch man arrested for racing on German motorway at 235km/h
World.content:
A Dutch man has been arrested for driving his Porsche 911 at speeds of up to 235 km/h on a German motorway while allegedly under the influence of cannabis.

The section of the A3 near Koblenz where he was stopped has no speed limit, but the 23-year-old man was pulled over for “extremely dangerous” driving after he weaved in and out of traffic and tailgated a police car.

A drug test revealed traces of THC, the active ingredient in cannabis, in his system. The man told police he ran a coffeeshop in Eindhoven with his father and regularly took the drug “for professional reasons”.

Police said traffic was relatively heavy for the time of day when the man was stopped just after midday on Monday. “It was only through good fortune that there were no traffic accidents,” they said.

The man has been charged with racing on the highway and dangerous driving. Police confiscated his driving licence and ordered him to pay €10,000 in bail before being released.

He was collected from the police station in Montabaur, 25km west of Koblenz, by his father.

In a separate incident across the border, a man from Rotterdam was arrested after reaching speeds of 246 km/h on the A15 while under the influence of drink and drugs.

The 40-year-old was stopped after passing a speed check near Papendrecht on Tuesday night on a section of motorway where the limit is 100 km/h.

His car was impounded and his licence seized by police after he was charged with dangerous driving and driving under the influence.

World.title: Fast food outlets almost double in under 20 years
World.content:

The Netherlands had 19,435 fast food outlets at the start of 2026, an increase of 88% since 2007, according to figures published on Wednesday by national statistics agency CBS.

The count covers cafeterias, sandwich shops, food stalls and ice cream parlours, which now make up slightly more than half of all the country’s 38,600 food outlets.

Restaurants grew more slowly over the same period, rising 73% from 11,055 to 19,165. Because fast food outlets expanded faster, they overtook restaurants in 2020 and have outnumbered them since.

Cities and the coast

Nearly 20% of all fast food outlets are in the four largest cities. Amsterdam has 1,605, Rotterdam 975, The Hague 790 and Utrecht 445.

Measured against population, however, the densest concentrations are not urban. The national average is close to 1.1 outlets per 1,000 residents, and it is tourist areas that push well beyond it.

Vlieland has 8.3 outlets per 1,000 residents, the highest in the country, followed by Schiermonnikoog on 4.1 and Terschelling on 3.1. Coastal municipalities in Zeeland, Zandvoort in Noord-Holland and Valkenburg aan de Geul in Zuid-Limburg also rank highly.

The east and northeast have fewer outlets per head than the national average. Staphorst in Overijssel has the fewest, at 0.3 per 1,000 residents, almost four times below the average.

World.title: NEC draw 0-0 at Olympiacos to boost Champions League hopes
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

NEC Nijmegen kept their hopes of a place in the Champions League alive with a 0-0 draw against Olympiacos in Greece.

The match was an even contest, with both teams notching up 10 chances over the 90 minutes.

The home side dominated the early exchanges, but Dick Schreuder’s side were stronger in the second half as Cape Verdean midfielder Jamiro Monteiro and Noé Lebreton went close for NEC.

Monteiro, newly signed from PEC Zwolle, replaced Japanese midfielder Kodai Sano, who was left out of the team at his own request pending his expected move to PSV Eindhoven for €14.5 million.

Former Ajax forward Dusan Tadic came on in the second half to make his debut for NEC at the age of 37, replacing the 35-year-old Bryan Linssen in the front line alongside the 38-year-old captain Tjaronn Chery.

It was NEC’s first taste of European football since a team coached by Mario Been lost 1-0 to HSV Hamburg in the UEFA Cup in 2009.

The two teams will play the return leg in Nijmegen’s Goffertstadion next Tuesday, August 11, with the winners going through to a play-off against either Union Saint-Gilloise of Belgium or Norwegian side Bødo/Glimt for a place in the lucrative group stages.

Poland has urged the European Union to adopt tougher measures in response to the recent migration crisis in Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. During a special meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Poland stressed its own experience with “weaponised” migration from Belarus and called for the EU to adopt a similar response, which has included a ban on nearly all asylum claims for people crossing irregularly. 🔵 KOMUNIKAT | Polska przedstawiła swoje stanowisko ws. migracji na nadzwyczajnym posiedzeniu Rady JHA w sprawie ostatnich wydarzeń w Ceucie 🇵🇱🇪🇺 Wiceminister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji @MaciekDuszczyk wziął udział w odbywającym się we wtorek (4 sierpnia br.)… pic.twitter.com/glfyiu5ZW3 — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) August 4, 2026 Last week, tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, most of them by swimming there from neighbouring Morocco. The incident prompted expressions of concern from many European leaders, including calls to restrict Spain’s participation in the Schengen free movement zone (despite the fact that anyone leaving Ceuta for the European mainland is subject to identity checks). Among those to speak out was Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who on Friday called on Spain to “follow our example if Schengen is to survive”. Poland has tightened asylum laws, border procedures, and has built effective barriers on its border with Belarus, which is the eastern border of the EU. We have invested billions of euros and engaged thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards. Spain must follow our… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 31, 2026 That was a reference to Poland’s response to a crisis on its eastern border, where since 2021 Belarus has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross irregularly into the EU. Both Poland and the EU have accused Belarus and its ally Russia of deliberately “weaponising” migration in an attempt to destabilise European societies as part of Moscow and Minsk’s broader “hybrid threats” against the EU. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has restricted the right to asylum, invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, and has deployed thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards there (who have also been given expanded rights to use firearms). A court has ruled that Poland's recently introduced partial suspension of the right to asylum is justified and lawful. It rejected a complaint by a Sudanese man who had been denied the right to claim asylum after crossing irregularly from Belarus https://t.co/jx3s1AxRgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2025 On Saturday, Tusk and 11 other EU leaders jointly signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. While they welcomed Spain’s cooperation with Morocco to send most of the migrants back, they also called for an extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers to “agree on a coordinated European response, including the rapid mobilisation of available EU instruments and the necessary support to Spain”. At that meeting, which took place on Tuesday, Poland’s interior ministry said that it had expressed the view that “illegal entry into the European Union should automatically exclude the possibility of obtaining residence permits, and therefore the possibility of permanent residence in the future”. While Poland’s statement did not mention it directly, earlier this year Spain’s government launched an amnesty that allowed undocumented migrants to apply to legalise their stay in the country. Over one million people had signed up for the scheme by the time it closed at the end of June. In its statement, Poland’s interior ministry warned that “migration must be fully controlled”, as otherwise it can “be used against the values that guide the EU”. It also called for the “official recognition of migration as a challenge directly linked to security”. Poland said that, at Monday’s meeting, it had “presented its own experiences with border protection in the context of the instrumentalisation and weaponisation of migration and adapting law to migration challenges”, including restrictions on asylum claims. “The example of Ceuta clearly demonstrates that absolute access to asylum is impossible to maintain in the face of such real threats,” wrote the interior ministry, which said that it “welcomed the shared perspective on migration among a growing number of member states”. In a statement of its own, the European Council noted that there had been a “common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight.” It added that member states “were united in expressing strong solidarity with Spain”, appreciated its “swift and effective efforts” to deal with the crisis, and had also expressed their condolences for the people who died while attempting to cross from Morocco to Ceuta. World.title: Unexploded WWII ordnance discovered under busy Warsaw street
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Part of central Warsaw was shut down today after unexploded ordnance from World War Two was found buried under a major road during construction work. The discovery, which came just days after the city commemorated the anniversary of its wartime uprising against Nazi-German occupation, led to traffic being diverted and residents being warned to stay away from their windows and avoid going outside while bomb disposal experts worked to safely remove the item. W Al. Solidarności znaleziono niewybuch, najprawdopodobniej z czasów II wojny światowej. ℹ️ Czytaj więcej: https://t.co/Fv6oe84XiM pic.twitter.com/BfjQPZveYZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 4, 2026 The object, reportedly around 70 centimetres long, was found early on Tuesday morning on Solidarity Avenue, a major thoroughfare, during modernisation work on tram lines. “We were digging a trench and I literally just touched it with the tip [of my digger],” the operator of the excavator who found it told broadcaster TVN. Staff working at the site were immediately evacuated to a safe distance. Police later confirmed that the item is unexploded ordnance, and that initial findings indicate it dates from World War Two. Bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene in the afternoon. However, they have not confirmed precisely what type of ordnance was discovered or its origin, reports Polsat News. Warsaw was the site of major fighting during World War Two, beginning in 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Poland. In 1943, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest single act of Jewish resistance during the war, took place. On 1 August 1944, the Polish underground Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising, which was the largest single act of armed resistance anywhere in German-occupied Europe during the war. In response, the Germans destroyed much of the city, around 85% of which lay in ruins by 1945. Warsaw’s historic Old Town was meticulously rebuilt after the war. But many other parts of the city were redeveloped by the newly installed communist authorities, including Solidarity Avenue (which during the communist era was named after Polish-Soviet Red Army General Karol Świerczewski). Thousands of vehicles drove over the unexploded ordnance every day for decades. “Warsaw is marked by history, and there are many such surprises,” Witold Urbanowicz, spokesman for the city’s tram operator, told news website Interia. After the fall of the Warsaw Uprising – which began 80 years ago today – the German occupiers expelled the city's entire population. However, some survivors decided to remain among the ruins. They became known as "Robinson Crusoes" and this is their story https://t.co/UuVbfbcpQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 1, 2024 Unexploded ordnance is regularly found in Poland. In May this year, around 200 anti-personnel mines dating from World War Two were discovered at the construction site of a student dormitory at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. In October last year, two men were hospitalised after an artillery shell that one of them had brought home from a forest exploded in his apartment while the pair were under the influence of alcohol. Earlier that year, wild boars unearthed 21 mortar shells buried in a forest since the war. In 2023, 72 unexploded artillery shells were discovered during renovation work at a primary school and four pieces of World War Two ordnance were found in the walls of a church undergoing renovation. Wild boars dug up 21 mortar shells from World War Two that had been buried in a Polish forest. The unexploded ordnance has now been safely removed without harm to either the animals or humans https://t.co/W9kaPr1BNw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
