Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.title: Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.content:
A river rafting tourist attraction in southwestern China has come under fire for offering “temporary girlfriends” and “very attractive” female companions who hold hands with, hug, and kiss customers while they raft.

Reported widely last week, the female companion service was offered by Luobei River Drifting, a popular rafting attraction in Guizhou province, beginning this summer. The rafting route, known for its thrilling rapids, lasts between 1.5 and 4 hours and covers up to 12.5 kilometers. Tickets cost up to 238 yuan ($35) per person.

In recent years, rafting attractions around China, including in the central Henan province, the eastern Jiangsu province, and the southern Hainan province, have launched scripted “NPC” rafting experiences, hiring workers to act as wolves, monkeys, bears, and frogs, as well as characters from the classic novel “Journey to the West” while customers raft. Related videos on Chinese social media have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

An undercover reporter at High Wind News, a platform under state-run media outlet Chinese Business View, posing as a customer contacted the attraction’s customer service on the messaging app WeChat, which informed them that they could choose from three service packages: a 398-yuan “highly attractive” companion who accompanies the rider with no additional physical contact, a 1,288-yuan partner with “upgraded appearance with polite physical contact,” and a 1,988-yuan “temporary girlfriend” option.

Customer service sent the reporter several photos — purported to be real pictures of the female companions — along with profiles of more than 30 women, including their height, weight, and age. Some photos were labeled “pure green,” indicating the companion’s service does not include “sexual behavior or contact.”

“The 1,988-yuan package is just like dating — you can hold hands, hug, and kiss,” the staff member told the undercover reporter, hinting that there could be further meetups after the initial rafting encounter.

“We create a legitimate setting for you to meet and communicate. We’re essentially just the intermediary,” the customer service representative added, claiming to receive around 400 groups of customers a day. The staff member also said the rafting park had more than 1,000 workers and required companions to be reserved in advance.

An account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by the name of “Luobei River NPC Scripted Drifting” had reportedly posted promotional videos of young women accompanying tourists during rafting and water activities, with slogans such as, “What heals you isn’t the scenery, but the emotional value.” The account has since been deleted.

Employees at the tourist attraction later confirmed to domestic media that companion services were available and directed reporters to the same customer service WeChat account.

In an official announcement posted on WeChat last Thursday, however, the company behind the park denied any connection to the female companion service, saying a separate company had privately launched the service.

A day later, on July 31, the local tourism bureau announced that Luobei River Drifting had agreed to collaborate with a management company specializing in upgraded rafting experiences, where tourists become the protagonists in stories instead of passive sightseers. According to the company’s official WeChat account, it had signed the cooperation agreement on May 6.

On July 31, the rafting operator was ordered by the local government to suspend operations for “rectification.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Female rafting companions. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018849/Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.title: Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018849/Out of the Blue: China Bans Lights Signaling Self-Driving Mode
World.content:
China has discontinued the blue exterior lights common to its vehicles equipped with autonomous driving features.

The ban, leaked by a car industry blogger on microblogging platform Weibo on July 29, was outlined in an official notice from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. According to the notice, the ban took effect as of July 27 for new vehicles, while existing vehicles are apparently not affected at this time.

The same day, the state-affiliated China Automotive Standardization Research Institute, while not directly confirming the ban, said on its public account on messaging app WeChat that the blue lights have been used excessively and improperly, and that a new national standard is under revision.

The blue lights, or advanced driver assistance system indicator lights, are usually found on the wing mirrors or lower front and back fenders of vehicles with advanced driver assistance systems. Introduced in 2022 by domestic car brand Li Auto, automakers began adopting them to indicate to other road users that intelligent driving systems were in use.

However, China’s current vehicle lighting standard does not include specific provisions for blue lights and permits only white, red, yellow, and amber for vehicle signal lights.

In its July 29 post, the China Automotive Standardization Research Institute said blue lights can cause glare for other road users at night, distracting them or interfering with their judgment of road conditions. It also noted that vehicles equipped with the lights are more likely to be cut off or followed closely by other drivers, increasing the risk of accidents.

In addition, many vehicles’ blue lights are installed in the car’s preexisting turn lamps, meaning that turn signals can sometimes glow blue.

An insider at Geely Automobile, China’s leading car manufacturer, confirmed to domestic media that they had indeed received notice of the ban but declined to disclose specific details. “We are aware of the news and will strictly comply with national regulations, awaiting further instructions from the government,” the insider said.

Zeng Qinglin, general manager of domestic car brand Yijing, listed what he sees as the reasons for the ban on his Weibo account. “First,” he said, “the brightness and flickering of various blue lights lack unified standards, affecting traffic safety and causing light pollution.”

“Second, other drivers, seeing blue lights on the car ahead, know it’s using an intelligent driving system and deliberately cut in, assuming the system will brake automatically,” he wrote. “As a result, drivers using the intelligent driving system are often startled by sudden braking. A device intended to signal safety has instead become a new source of risk.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Blue lights on a car indicating self-driving mode. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018838/How China Delivers a 14-Yuan Bouquet Over 2,000 Kilometers
World.title: How China Delivers a 14-Yuan Bouquet Over 2,000 Kilometers
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018838/How China Delivers a 14-Yuan Bouquet Over 2,000 Kilometers
World.content:
On China’s major e-commerce platforms, a bouquet of fresh-cut roses from the southwestern Yunnan province sells for just 14 yuan ($2), with free delivery to most parts of the country.

For consumers, this is an ordinary online purchase: tap to pay on a phone screen, then wait for the flowers to arrive at the door. But behind that simple transaction is a complex logistical challenge. Cut flowers are highly perishable. They lose moisture quickly and must travel more than 2,000 kilometers from Yunnan to major cities like Shanghai. Harvesting, sorting, packing, transportation, and last-mile delivery all have to happen within a narrow window.

How can a product worth less than 20 yuan cover the costs of packaging and inter-provincial delivery while remaining affordable as an everyday online purchase? The answer lies in how far China’s supply chain has evolved.

The first factor is scale.

In 2025, China’s express delivery companies handled 198.95 billion parcels, or nearly 550 million per day. Around 90% were shipped between different cities or regions.

Such enormous volumes allow logistics companies to build fixed routes, operate frequent departures, and invest in large-scale sorting centers. The costs of warehouses, vehicles, information systems, and automation equipment can be distributed across hundreds of millions of parcels.

In cities with dense order volumes, trucks can consolidate packages heading to the same areas, while couriers can complete more deliveries along compact routes. Adding another parcel does not require rebuilding the entire logistics system from scratch. Instead, existing infrastructure becomes more efficient as volume increases.

But scale alone is not enough. A huge number of parcels can also create new problems, including congested warehouses, idle vehicles, and inventory stored in the wrong places.

What has made China’s logistics system distinctive is its size coupled with the widespread application of supply chain management.

Other countries also use supply chain management, but China has applied it in a market with a combination of scale, density, complexity, and cost pressures rarely seen elsewhere. It has turned complex logistics systems into everyday services that even low-priced goods can use.

One example is demand forecasting.

As parcel volumes increase, companies need to predict not only what products consumers will buy but also where demand will come from and how much inventory and transport capacity each region will require.

This is why presales have become increasingly important, especially during China’s major shopping festivals. Rather than waiting for consumers to place orders on the day of a promotion, platforms use presales to collect advance commitments from buyers.

This gives retailers a clearer picture of expected sales volumes and buyer locations. They can prepare inventory, organize picking and packing, and adjust sales plans ahead of time. Logistics companies can reserve warehouse space and transportation capacity before order volumes surge.

Presales are only one forecasting tool. Companies also analyze historical sales, browsing trends, promotional plans, and real-time orders to estimate demand. The goal is to prepare resources before a sudden increase in orders overwhelms the system.

But predicting demand is only the first step. Goods must also be placed in the right locations — this is the warehousing question of supply chain management.

While forecasting has become increasingly sophisticated, China’s warehousing capacity has also expanded significantly. But warehousing is not simply about the size and number of facilities. Location is also crucial because it determines how far goods must travel after an order is placed and how many transfers are needed before reaching consumers. Logistics costs depend not only on how quickly goods move, but also on where inventory is positioned.

Take the major e-commerce platform JD.com as an example. In the first half of 2026, JD Logistics expanded its fulfillment network by opening new warehouses in the eastern Shandong province and other regions. Its domestic network now includes more than 3,600 warehouses across over 2,800 county-level areas, allowing merchants to stock goods closer to consumers and fulfill orders from nearby facilities.

In the past, deliveries during major shopping festivals could take weeks. Today, some presold goods are moved in advance to regional distribution hubs. Once buyers near these warehouses make the final payment, delivery can begin almost immediately, with some orders reportedly arriving within hours of payment.

For manufactured goods or everyday household items, placing inventory close to major consumer markets reduces delivery distances and logistics costs. Fresh produce, however, requires a different, more technology-intensive kind of logistics system.

Returning to Yunnan’s cut flowers, the challenge lies in speed and coordination.

At a fresh-flower cold-chain distribution center in Kunming, Yunnan’s provincial capital, five sorting lines operate at high speed. Automated equipment identifies each shipment’s destination and directs it onto the appropriate route. The center can process around 20,000 flower parcels per hour, with each parcel sorted in as little as three minutes — 1.5 times the efficiency of manual sorting.

The center began operations in 2021 and underwent a major upgrade in 2024. Its daily flower shipments increased from an initial 2 tons to more than 260 tons. After sorting, flowers quickly enter a transport network combining air freight, high-speed rail, and refrigerated trucks. Express air services can reach more than 28 cities within 24 hours, and over 90% of China’s major cities nationwide within 48 hours.

The logistics system behind fresh flowers is far more than simply transporting a box from one city to another. It is a complete chain covering harvesting, pre-cooling, sorting, packing, cold-chain transport, and final delivery. The goal of this system is to minimize transfers and reduce the time flowers spend outside controlled conditions.

Refrigeration, protective packaging, and air transport all increase costs. But for products whose value declines with every delay, faster and more controlled delivery reduces damage and extends their selling life.

This is why the key post-harvest steps, including pre-cooling, grading, and packing, must happen close to the farm, without delay. Origin-based sorting and cold-chain hubs allow flowers from multiple producers to be collected, processed, and shipped efficiently, transforming fragmented agricultural production into a reliable supply chain.

Demand forecasting, inventory positioning, warehouse placement, and AI-enabled dispatching may appear to be separate processes. In reality, they work together toward the same goal: reducing unnecessary waiting and avoiding inefficient movement.

What consumers ultimately see is often only a modest delivery fee, or simply a “free shipping” label. That price is not the result of a single cheap step. It reflects the coordination of order processing, inventory management, warehousing, transportation, and last-mile delivery.

This is the result of supply chain management applied at scale: a system that allows consumers across China to experience the increasingly ordinary reality of placing an order and receiving it almost instantly.

The 14-yuan bouquet of roses is therefore more than a cheap online purchase. It represents a shift in how people shop and access goods across one of the world’s largest consumer markets. The supply chain design behind it is what allows these expectations of convenience, speed, and choice to become an everyday reality.

Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A worker transports flower bouquets at a warehouse at the Dounan Flower Market, Kunming, Yunnan province, February 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018842/Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.title: Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018842/Chinese Village’s Viral Cicada Harvest Comes Under Fire
World.content:
In an eastern Chinese village, harvesting cicada nymphs for consumption has evolved from a seasonal tradition into a lucrative side business for farmers, fueled by a local official’s livestreaming business. But critics are questioning whether the trade is flourishing at the expense of local ecosystems.

This summer, Liu Lei, a village official of Dongjiezhuang Village in the eastern Shandong province, began selling wild cicada nymphs through livestreaming, sourcing the insects from locals. In the past week, he has come under fire online, with social media users citing environmental concerns.

Known in Chinese as zhiliaohou, or “cicada monkeys,” nymphs — immature, wingless cicadas who emerge after three to five years feeding on plant matter underground — have long been considered a summer delicacy in northern and eastern China. Historical texts, including the sixth-century agricultural encyclopedia “Qimin Yaoshu,” describe consumption of the insects in the region.

Liu, one of a growing number of village official influencers, markets local specialties and agricultural products such as honey and peaches on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, to boost the local economy.

Liu’s videos show villagers — largely seniors — going out each night at dusk, armed with flashlights and plastic bags, to search for the insects in the nearby forest. They then sell their collections to Liu at a designated point in the village for extra income. Each cicada sells for around 1 yuan ($0.14).

One 60-year-old local said he had caught more than 200 cicada nymphs in a single night. “I usually don’t eat them myself. One cicada nymph is priced higher than an ear of corn,” he said.

Liu’s actions have triggered debate online. While some support him for bringing in income for farmers, others argue that livestreaming has transformed a long-standing tradition into a commercial rush. Experts also warn that large-scale collection could threaten biodiversity and disrupt local food chains.

In an interview with local media, Liu said villagers have harvested cicada nymphs for decades without damaging the environment. “We have a tradition of only collecting nymphs that have just emerged from the soil,” he said. “Once they’ve molted into adult cicadas, no one catches them because they are no longer edible.”

Although Cryptotympana atrata, the preferred cicada species being collected, is not nationally protected, entomologists warn that large-scale population decimation could still affect local ecosystems.

Zhao Li, curator of the Insect Museum of West China in Chengdu, capital of the southwestern Sichuan province, told local media that cicadas help recycle nutrients in forests and provide food for birds and other wildlife. Their shed exoskeletons, Zhao added, are also widely used in traditional Chinese medicine.

Authorities have attempted to curb the collection of cicadas in some regions. In 2024, forestry officials in Tongchuan, a city in the northwestern Shaanxi province, warned against unauthorized harvesting of cicadas in forests and protected areas, stating that large-scale collection could damage vegetation, increase wildfire risks, and violate forestry regulations.

Specifically addressing the Dongjiezhuang Village case in a video posted to Douyin, Li Mingli, chairman of agricultural brand consulting firm Beijing Fangyuan, noted that, “Livestream traffic can amplify demand far beyond what unwritten local customs can regulate.”

Li suggested that instead of harvesting wild cicadas, the village could build a cicada farm, providing locals with a more stable source of income while reducing pressure on wild populations. He added that local authorities could also introduce collection quotas and rotate harvesting areas.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018839/China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.title: China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018839/China’s Elderly Embrace an Unlikely New Sport: Hyrox Races
World.content:
ZHEJIANG, East China — Wang Hui, a 68-year-old from Beijing, used to avoid intense exercise whenever possible. The retiree’s fitness regime mostly consisted of the odd brisk walk, and maybe a few leg raises at home.

But that suddenly changed a few months ago, when her daughter informed her she’d signed Wang up for a Hyrox race.

The fitness craze, which originated in Germany a few years ago, is not for the faint of heart: participants must complete eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by a set of strength exercises ranging from lunges to pushing a heavy sled.

Curious and keen to connect with her daughter — a long-time fitness enthusiast — Wang threw herself into training, building up from 1-kilometer jogs to 8-kilometer runs in just two months.

Then, one day in July, Wang found herself walking alongside her daughter into a cavernous expo center in the eastern city of Hangzhou packed with more than 6,000 competitors and 7,000 cheering spectators.

As she stood under the pulsing strobe lights, ears throbbing from the pumping bass, Wang could not have felt more out of her comfort zone. But she suspects that was her daughter’s intention all along.

“My daughter keeps surprising me,” she told Sixth Tone after completing the event in July. “She shows me, ‘I can still do this,’ ‘I can still do that.’”

Wang is far from alone. As Hyrox explodes in popularity across China, the races have unexpectedly begun to attract an ever greater number of retirees — many of them competing in their first event well after turning 70.

For some, the races represent a fresh challenge or an excuse to get fit. For others, like Wang, they offer a chance to reconnect with adult children for whom Hyrox has become a new obsession.

Even by global standards, Hyrox has taken off in China at astonishing speed. The first official Chinese Hyrox race took place as recently as 2024, with 1,700 fitness enthusiasts competing in a hall in Beijing.

Now, events are held all over the country, with early-bird registration often selling out within minutes despite costing up to 800 yuan ($125) for an individual entry fee — more than three times the entry fee for a typical marathon in China. At a recent race in Shanghai, over 10,000 people took part.

As elsewhere, Hyrox fans in China tend to be young, middle-class, and super-fit. Local races are filled with ripped 20- and 30-somethings working in competitive industries such as finance and artificial intelligence.

On Chinese social media, Hyrox’s appeal to such high-fliers has become a running joke. Users often quip that the sport taps into a deep Chinese love for hard work and standardized tests. Some even liken Hyrox training to preparing for the gaokao, China’s grueling college entrance exams.

But the sport also has a more inclusive side. At some events, participants can sign up in teams of two or more — allowing them to divide the workload — and the lack of cut-off time means slower competitors can complete the race.

That has opened the door to a growing number of elderly contenders. Online, there has been a wave of social media posts in recent months from Chinese millennials sharing their experiences of entering Hyrox races alongside their aging parents, many of them attracting thousands of likes.

Wang’s daughter, Xie Shanshan, is part of that trend. Now in her 40s, she took up running years ago while living and working in Beijing — competing in several half-marathons — before pivoting to Hyrox as the sport began to gain traction.

For Xie, the hope was that competing in the team event with her mother would give them a shared experience. But she also aimed to give Wang — who has been retired for years — a healthy jolt.

And she appears to have succeeded. After the initial shock wore off, Wang fully committed to the training and finished the Hangzhou race, with Xie reminding her to pace herself.

“We didn’t go at 100% effort,” Wang said. “My daughter kept saying, ‘Steady, steady, it’s about the taking part, not speed.’”

When asked whether it’s a good idea for seniors to participate in such high-intensity sports, Wang said it was easy to fall into a rut after retirement, spending all day scrolling social media or watching TV.

“But if you can step out and join social activities with younger people, your thinking and values get reenergized,” she said. “The real appeal lies in connecting with the younger generation, adding vitality to life, and broadening horizons.”

Other child-parent teams competing in Hangzhou shared similar experiences. Yu Lian, a 45-year-old CrossFit enthusiast, had been training for nearly a decade and had already run solo in two Hyrox races.

But after seeing online that some of her favorite fitness influencers had brought their parents along to Hyrox events, she decided to ask her 74-year-old father to join her at her next race.

According to Yu, he immediately replied: “Just tell me what to do, and I’ll do it. I walk so much every day. I’m already the number one in our neighborhood!”

Though Yu had emphasized “safety first,” her father took the training unexpectedly seriously. For nearly two months, he took brisk walks outside several times a week, and ended up losing 5 kilograms.

On race day, it was a similar story. Yu’s plan was to do all the strength exercises herself, while her father walked alongside her. But he ended up getting far more involved than she had expected.

After each kilometer run, she found him already waiting for her at the work station, arm outstretched, ready to pull her forward. In the final event — the “wall ball,” where competitors have to throw a heavy medicine ball against a wall — her father, fueled by the crowd’s energy, grabbed a ball and nailed the target on the second attempt.

For Yu, the race came to feel like an important bonding experience. Growing up, her relationship with her father had always been reserved — love was expressed through deeds, not words, she recalled.

The term “parent-child bonding” usually conjures up images of young families with small children, but Yu said she felt that older generations — those in their 40s and 70s — needed it just as much.

“Interactions between adult children and aging parents are often limited,” Yu said. “Participation in the race is a meaningful way to foster various types of connection.”

Yet, for all its emotional benefits, Hyrox can be a dangerous activity — especially for a beginner in their 60s or 70s. Li Cong, a functional training, pilates, and sports rehabilitation instructor in Shanghai, warned the sport presented a high injury risk.

“After running, the small stabilizing muscles around our joints fatigue,” she said. “When we then do weighted sled pushes or kettlebell exercises, the lower back and knees are forced to compensate and bear all the weight. When your form breaks down under fatigue, the injury rate is much higher than if you trained running and strength separately.”

Sun Yang, a senior rehabilitation therapist in the sports medicine department at Shanghai’s Huashan Hospital, echoed those concerns. A Hyrox devotee herself, she approaches training with caution.

“I stop and rest for a few days if I feel any discomfort,” Sun said. “I don’t allow myself to continue exercising while overtired or in pain.”

Wang Zheng — no relation to Wang Hui — thought long and hard before inviting his mother to form a Hyrox team with him.

As a 32-year-old fitness professional, Wang Zheng had already competed in 22 Hyrox events, and he was keen to bring his mother, Ma Jing, into his world. But he also knew that the traditional, hardcore format wasn’t a fit for everyone.

Luckily, the mixed-doubles category offered a solution. “In mixed doubles, I can take on 90% of the workload, and there is no cut-off time at the venue. That meant I could finally bring my mom along to play,” he said.

Ma, a 65-year-old retiree living in eastern China’s Shandong province, was initially apprehensive when her son suggested entering a race together. “I was actually a bit scared, afraid of embarrassing him,” she recalled.

But her fear soon gave way to a deeper motivation. “I don’t want to be a burden to my son as I get older, and the first step is to stay healthy,” Ma said. “So I thought, let me challenge myself.”

The training ended up having a profound impact on Ma. She moved in with her son in the southern city of Shenzhen months before the race so that they could prepare together, and watching his tough routine gave her a new understanding of his commitment.

His dedication also inspired Ma to take her own training seriously. In November, the pair completed the race in Shanghai in 100 minutes, with Ma’s performance surpassing her son’s expectations. The atmosphere even motivated her to take on several exercises that she had never tried before.

Now, flush with her triumph, she has decided to push on with her training. She runs 5 to 10 kilometers a day, hits the gym for strength training 20 days a month, and is lining up her next races.

“Since I’ve decided to compete, I have to show up in my best form,” she said.

More importantly, Ma said Hyrox had helped shatter her self-doubt. “I used to think I wasn’t ready, but actually, we don’t need to prepare for everything. Just participating is a reward in itself.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran.

(Header image: Elderly participants in Hyrox races. Xie Anran/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018829/The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.title: The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018829/The Chinese Tea That Became a British Joke — and Those That Didn’t
World.content:
This is the second article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED). Read Part 1.

China is the origin of tea, and its global vocabulary remains deeply rooted in Chinese. The English word “tea” derives from the Minnan (Hokkien) dialect, reflecting maritime trade routes that carried the leaf from the coastal ports of China’s eastern Fujian province to Europe. Meanwhile, “char” (or “cha”), originating from Mandarin or Cantonese, persists in British slang as a colloquial term for a cup of tea. More recently, the Indian-derived “chai” — a popular blend of black tea, milk, sugar or honey, and spices — has gained traction in Western coffee shops. Yet the foundational lexicon of tea in English remains unmistakably Chinese.

While China produces a wide array of premium teas, English dictionaries have historically been highly selective in what they adopt. Among the commonly accepted lists of China’s most celebrated teas, only Wuyi rock tea (Bohea) and Keemun black tea (Keemun) traditionally made the cut, both transliterated from regional names. However, a closer reading of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) reveals a more expansive linguistic landscape: nearly 30 Chinese tea terms have been formally incorporated into English. Some are widely used, while others survive as lexical relics. This lexicon includes foundational terms such as green tea, white tea, oolong, and congou; premium black teas like pekoe, souchong, and Lapsang souchong; historic green teas including Hyson and Singlo; post-fermented varieties such as Pu-erh; and descriptive terms such as pearl tea (gunpowder tea) and imperial tea.

Within this OED-derived lexicon of Chinese tea terms in English, one striking anomaly stands out: the theatrical caricature of “Widow Twankey.” The linguistic transformation began in Tunxi, a historic tea hub in the eastern Anhui province. The city’s name was phonetically adapted into “Twankay” to denote large quantities of green tea exported from the region during the 18th century. As this tea became associated with lower grades in Western markets because of its older, coarser, and more ragged leaves, “Twankay” was later repurposed by playwrights into the comedic character “Widow Twankey,” and eventually entered British slang as a term for cheap gin.

In 1861, playwright H.J. Byron named Aladdin’s mother “Widow Twankey” to imply she was “past her best.” The character went on to become a pantomime staple — a bawdy, eccentric “dame” traditionally played by a man in drag, often depicted running a chaotic Chinese laundry in a fictionalized “Old Peking.”

For modern readers, the fact that a Chinese tea term was transformed into a theatrical punchline can come as a shock. Yet placed within the broader OED record, Twankey remains a clear exception. The vast majority of Chinese tea terms in English have been treated with linguistic and cultural respect.

Take Bohea (Wuyi tea), for instance. As one of the earliest black teas imported into Britain in the early 1700s, OED citations show it was initially regarded as a luxury product. Although its commercial standing later declined — by the mid-19th century it was classified among lower-grade black teas — its literary presence remained stable. From Alexander Pope to William Makepeace Thackeray, Bohea continued to appear in print as an authentic beverage.

Similarly, congou (gongfu tea) was established as a marker of upper-class refinement. In Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s 1777 comedic play “The School for Scandal,” congou appears alongside exotic luxuries such as avadavats (tropical songbirds) and Indian crackers. Victorian dietary writers later formalized this hierarchy. In his 1874 “A Treatise on Food and Dietetics,” F.W. Pavy explicitly ranked major black teas in ascending order of quality: Bohea, oolong, congou, campoi.

This documentary respect extends to souchong and Lapsang souchong. In the 18th century, souchong was among the most expensive “brown teas” (the contemporary term for what is now called black tea), attracting such attention that it was subjected to chemical analysis by the Royal Society. Lapsang souchong, despite its distinctive smoky profile, was embraced by intellectual circles. Samuel Beckett praised the “choicest lapsang souchong,” while Aldous Huxley and Iris Murdoch incorporated it naturally into their writing. The OED also records its organic evolution in everyday speech, recording spelling variations like “lapseng,” “lapsang soochong,” and “lapsang suchong.”

The same holds true for pekoe. As early as 1713, essayist Joseph Addison listed it alongside coffee and chocolate as a fashionable social staple, while East India Company records documented its premium trade value. From the tinfoiled chests of “flowery Pekoe” described by G.A. Sala in 1859 to the “teak-colored pekoe” poured in Annie Proulx’s 1993 novel “The Shipping News,” pekoe has maintained a continuous literary and commercial presence. Gunpowder tea, tightly rolled into pellets, was elegantly translated by early British scholars as “pearl tea.”

Importantly, this documentary trail is not limited to black teas. Hyson, known in Chinese as xichun, was championed by Thomas Jefferson, who preferred “young Hyson” for its strength and flavor. By 1948, The New York Times described young Hyson and pinhead gunpowder as the “aristocrats of green teas.”

Singlo was once a major commercial variety in the 18th century, with East India Company ledgers recording millions of pounds imported annually. Known in Chinese as Songluo, after the Songluo Mountain in Anhui where it originates, it was so highly prized that travelers noted authentic batches had become exceedingly rare, with counterfeit versions flooding the market.

Even the obsolete terms in the OED offer a fascinating philosophical counterpoint. Imperial, for instance, once described by J.M. Walsh in 1892 as “the perfection of tea,” has since fallen out of use. Similarly, bing has vanished from common usage. First documented by the Royal Society in 1702 as “the second growth in April,” it is a dialect romanization of the Chinese character “ming” (meaning “bright”), evoking the clarity of early spring after Qingming. Another example, “Oopack,” a highly valued tea from the central Hubei province that fetched top auction prices in The Times as late as 1855, now survives only as a rare lexical relic.

Today, the translation of Chinese tea culture continues to evolve. While traditional teas such as Longjing (Dragon Well) remain largely untranslated in English, modern milk tea brands are experimenting with hybrid naming strategies. Chagee (drawing on “cha,” the Chinese word for tea, and “gee” (which approximates the sound of the Chinese character ji – a classical Chinese term for female performers) and ChaPanda merge Chinese linguistic cues with global marketing logic.

Meanwhile, a new wave of tea culture is reshaping global consumption. Bubble tea (boba), which originated in Taiwan in the 1980s, has become a global phenomenon. What began as a simple blend of black tea, milk, and chewy tapioca pearls has evolved into a highly customizable, brightly colored drink embedded in global youth culture. Driven by social media aesthetics and its distinctive texture, boba has moved from East Asian diaspora spaces into mainstream cafés worldwide, reshaping expectations of what tea can be.

Similarly, yum cha, the Cantonese tradition of drinking tea with dim sum, remains strong across global cities, functioning as a social anchor in urban dining culture. Beyond this, yin yeung — the Hong Kong-style blend of milk tea and coffee — is also gradually capturing international attention. As this bold, caffeinated fusion finds its way onto menus outside Hong Kong, it signals the ongoing global influence of hybridized regional drinks.

This modern expansion is part of a broader global tea renaissance that also includes the Indian-derived chai, now a staple in Western coffee chains. From the early days of Singlo and Imperial to the modern ubiquity of boba and yin yeung, Chinese tea has left a lasting mark on the English language. The theatrical figure of Widow Twankey remains an outlier, a historical distortion rather than a defining pattern.

Yet tea’s vitality has never been confined to its point of origin. A beverage rooted solely in China would have remained culturally rich but geographically limited; its global life depends on circulation, adaptation, and reinterpretation. Today, as global consumers fall in love with tea, they continue to reshape it into new forms, from South Asia’s spiced chai to Southeast Asia’s milk tea variations and contemporary café experiments in the West.

It is this ongoing exchange and reinvention that sustains tea’s global relevance. Ultimately, its legacy is not only Chinese heritage embedded in language, but a shared cultural system in motion — a cup that grows richer with every new tradition poured into it.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Imee Marcos, state auditor clash over Sara Duterte’s accountability for confidential funds
World.content:
Screenshot from the Senate of the Philippines

IMPEACHMENT COURT. State auditor and witness Roderick Wamil answers Senator-judge Imee Marcos' questions during the 13th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on August 5, 2026.

On the sidelines, one of Senator Imee Marcos' staff is heard suggesting that she cite the witness — state auditor Roderick Wamil — in contempt

MANILA, Philippines – A heated exchange erupted between Senator-judge Imee Marcos and state auditor and witness Roderick Wamil during the 13th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

On Wednesday, August 5, Marcos questioned Wamil on who should be considered the accountable officer for confidential funds. But her question comes with an argument.

A known ally of the Vice President, Marcos argued that Duterte was not the payee of the cash advances funded by the confidential funds.

Citing the joint circular governing confidential and intelligence funds, Marcos said the accountable officers were former Office of the Vice President (OVP) special disbursing officer Gina Acosta and former Department of Education special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda.

“Not entirely correct, Your Honor,” Wamil replied.

Inside the courtroom, the staff of senator-judges exchanged glances. There were murmurs.

Wamil explained that while designated officers are accountable for the cash advances they receive, the joint circular also assigns responsibility to the head of the agency to approve the cash advances and oversee the proper utilization of confidential funds. He added that Duterte also signed certifications attesting to the confidential fund transactions.

Marcos attempted to interrupt Wamil as he continued his explanation.

On the sidelines of the plenary, one of Marcos’ staff was heard suggesting that the senator cite the witness in contempt. “Ma’am, i-cite mo na ‘yan ng contempt (Ma’am, cite him in contempt),” he said.

Her staff even stood up and whispered to Marcos, who at the time was standing before the podium.

“Kanina mo pa ko inaaway (You have been arguing with me),” Marcos told Wamil.

Presiding officer Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero stepped in to diffuse the tension, asking Wamil to “avoid arguing” with the senator-judges.

Wamil apologized.

Later, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros asked Wamil who should be considered accountable officials under the Government Accounting Code.

Wamil, a lawyer and certified public accountant, said accountability extends beyond the disbursing officer and also covers the head of the agency.

Gaps in auditing?

During the interpellation, several senator-judges pointed out the flaws in policies surrounding auditing in the country.

Senator-judges Ping Lacson, Erwin Tulfo, and Win Gatchalian asked whether the Commission on Audit (COA) had attempted to verify if the signatories in the acknowledgment receipts used real names or aliases.

Wamil said an auditor’s role is limited to determining whether an agency’s liquidation documents comply with documentary requirements. It does not include verifying the identities of the recipients.

He also said the joint circular neither expressly allows nor prohibits the use of aliases in acknowledgment receipts.

Senator-judge Bam Aquino then asked Duterte’s legal counsel, Michael Poa, whether the names appearing in the acknowledgment receipts submitted by the OVP were real. Poa declined to answer, saying it was part of the defense’s “legal strategy” and would be addressed at the appropriate time.

Lacson also pointed out that COA auditors do not have security clearances, limiting their ability to conduct deeper investigations or independently verify the identities of the signatories.

During his testimony, Wamil said one of the documentary requirements in auditing confidential fund disbursements for payment of information is “evidence of success.”

Lacson, a former Philippine National Police chief, argued that the guidelines appear to leave a gap. He asked how COA determines whether an intelligence operation was unsuccessful when the auditing rules require proof of success.

Wamil also testified that the Duterte-led OVP failed to submit several required supporting documents for its confidential fund transactions.

Hontiveros, meanwhile, asked whether the OVP’s use of P24.93 million in confidential funds for medicines classified as “payment of reward” was a normal practice.

Wamil, who said he had audited the confidential fund spending of more than 30 national government agencies and numerous local government units, replied that it was not normal for a government agency to purchase medicines as a form of reward.

Senator-judge Robin Padilla, for his part, argued that the Department of Education’s confidential funds under Duterte helped curb alleged communist recruitment in schools and prevented planned attacks.

Wamil declined to comment, saying the matter was outside his expertise and personal knowledge.

Meanwhile, Senator Loren Legarda did not attend the trial again, bringing her absences to three consecutive days.

This comes after the Office of the Ombudsman announced the pending plunder and graft complaints against her and her son, Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste, over the latter’s solar energy projects. – Rappler.com

World.title: Long overdue IRR for early childhood care law finally signed
World.content:
IRR SIGNING. Education Secretary Sonny Angara and Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla lead the signing of the implementing rules and regulations of the Early Childhood Care and Development System Act on August 5, 2026.

The implementing rules and regulations are signed over a year after Republic Act No. 12199 was enacted into law in May 2025

MANILA, Philippines – The government took a step forward in strengthening early childhood care and development (ECCD) services in the country by signing the implementing rules and regulations (IRR) of Republic Act No. 12199.

It was, however, a year late. The ECCD System Act was enacted into law in May 2025, with the IRR deadline set in August last year.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, and ECCD Council Vice Chairperson and Executive Director Teresita Inciong signed the framework to implement the law on Wednesday, August 5.

It is much needed after the country recorded a stunting rate of 25.3% in 2025, up from 23.6% in 2023, according to the Food and Nutrition Research Institute. This is the first increase in 10 years.

The law strengthens the country’s ECCD system, expanding access to health, nutrition, and quality early learning for children from birth to eight years old.

UNESCO previously said that investing in early childhood care and education “yields a 13% return through improved health, economic outcomes, and social cohesion.”

The law also mandates the creation of child development centers in every barangay. It is a facility where children five years old and below are cared for during part of the day by ECCD service providers.

Around 4,600 barangays in the country still have no child development centers, according to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2).

ECCD service providers include child development teachers and child development workers. The law states that plantilla positions must be created for them.

In its news release, the Department of Education (DepEd) said the IRR provides clear guidelines for local government units to institutionalize local ECCD offices, professionalize child development workers through plantilla creation, and execute localized ECCD roadmaps aligned with the national strategy.

“The DepEd emphasizes that strengthening foundational learning begins long before a child enters formal schooling,” the agency said. “By promoting early literacy and numeracy and holistic child development during the early years, the ECCD System Act lays the groundwork for improved learning outcomes throughout basic education.”

More funding for ECCD sought

For its part, advocacy group Philippine Business for Education (PBEd) urged the government to earmark a “significant and protected share” for ECCD in the national budget.

In its 2026 State of Philippine Education report, PBEd also said the government must ensure that on-ground workers such as child development workers and barangay health workers are properly equipped and have the necessary support.

PBEd executive director Hanibal Camua stressed that investing in the first 1,000 days of children and supporting their literacy during early grade levels may lead to more proficient graduates from the basic education system.

Angara acknowledged the need to boost funding.

“Maganda na ‘yung feeding program natin sa Kinder at Grade 1, but we need to catch children at ages zero to five. Kasi pagpasok sa kindergarten, much of the damage has already been done,” he said in a chance interview on the sidelines of an event in Quezon City, ahead of the signing of the IRR.

(Our feeding program for Kinder and Grade 1 has already improved, but we need to catch children at ages zero to five. Once they enter kindergarten, much of the damage has already been done.)

Angara also said that only up to 29% of children aged three to four years old are in child development centers, and being fed by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).

Play Video

For this year, the DepEd has P25 billion for its school-based feeding program nationwide. However, it only targets universal feeding for kindergarten and Grade 1 public school students, and learners in Grades 2 to 6 that are found to be “wasted” and “severely wasted.”

Wasting, which means a child is too thin for their height, is a form of undernutrition.

According to the DepEd, there is a P1-billion allocation under the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) to establish child development centers in fourth- and fifth-class municipalities or low-income areas. EDCOM 2 earlier pushed for P2.46 billion.

The LGSF also includes funds for the initial creation of plantilla positions for child development workers in those areas.

Other ECCD-related funds in the 2026 budget are:

P226.9-million allocation for a scholarship program to upskill current child development workers under the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority

P9.6-billion funding for the DSWD’s Supplemental Feeding Program, providing hot meals and milk to three- to five-year-old kids in child development centers for 180 days

– Rappler.com
